summary: The article gives general Serbian wine history and geography but does not reproduce chart 46, the 2025 cultivar shares or the Merlot–Cabernet Sauvignon–Chardonnay–Grašac order.
notes: Individual Russian cultivar articles confirm international identities but not the Serbian register ranking.

title: Croatian Wikipedia search — Serbian vineyard rank and Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Graševina
summary: No Croatian Wikipedia article or passage was found that reproduces Serbia's end-2025 commercial Vineyard Register ranking; cultivar pages establish international use but not the Serbian percentages.
notes: The current Serbian Ministry chart is outside the available Croatian Wikipedia coverage.

title: English Wikipedia — Serbian wine and seven local or regional cultivars
provenance: Requested English Wikipedia corpus and linked cultivar searches
summary: The national article and cultivar pages give identity and general Serbian presence for several listed grapes but do not reproduce CEVVIN's publication date, commercial-area ranks or mean vineyard sizes for any of the seven.
notes: Wikipedia silence on parcel statistics neither confirms nor contradicts the institutional survey.

title: German Wikipedia — Weinbau in Serbien and cultivar searches
summary: German Wikipedia discusses Serbian regional cultivars and has detailed pages for some identities, but no article gives the seven CEVVIN national ranks, mean Serbian commercial-vineyard sizes or the underlying survey cutoff.
notes: Older national area figures in the article are methodologically incompatible with the CEVVIN means and ranks.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia search — Serbia ranks and mean parcel sizes for seven cultivars
summary: No Hungarian Wikipedia material was found that reproduces the CEVVIN commercial-area ranking or mean Serbian vineyard area for Prokupac, Smederevka, Vranac, Tamjanika, Slankamenka/Plovdina, Tamjanika crna or Kavčina.
notes: Hungarian cultivar articles can clarify some synonyms but not these Serbian survey values.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Виноградарство у Србији and cultivar list
summary: The article lists most relevant cultivars grown in Serbia but supplies no ranked commercial-area table, no mean parcel sizes and no citation to the CEVVIN 2019 publication.
notes: An unranked cultivar list cannot validate ordinals or arithmetic means.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Виноделие в Сербии and cultivar searches
summary: Russian Wikipedia provides general Serbian wine and cultivar context but none of the seven commercial-area ranks, mean vineyard sizes or CEVVIN survey-date metadata.
notes: The quantitative paragraph therefore depends on the named Serbian institutional source.

title: Croatian Wikipedia search — Serbia ranks and mean parcel sizes for seven cultivars
summary: No Croatian Wikipedia passage was found that reproduces CEVVIN's Serbian commercial-area ranks or mean vineyard sizes for the seven grapes.
notes: Croatian pages on Graševina, Pamid-related names or Muscat forms do not supply the requested Serbian statistics.

title: CEVVIN — Publications catalogue
provenance: Official Serbian Centre for Viticulture and Winemaking publication index
summary: Dates Autohtone i regionalne sorte vinove loze Srbije to 2019 and identifies CEVVIN as publisher, but exposes no survey reference date on the landing page.
notes: A 10 August 2019 industry notice confirms release and says printing was supported through a 2018 Ministry programme, which reinforces the need not to assume the data cutoff from publication year alone.

title: CEVVIN — Prokupac
provenance: Official CEVVIN cultivar and commercial-vineyard profile
summary: Explicitly reports ninth place by represented commercial area and a mean commercial-vineyard size of 0.11 ha for Prokupac.
notes: The profile does not show the precise survey cutoff or a downloadable underlying table.

title: CEVVIN — Smederevka
provenance: Official CEVVIN cultivar and commercial-vineyard profile
summary: Explicitly reports twelfth place by represented commercial area and a mean commercial-vineyard size of 0.14 ha for Smederevka.
notes: Scope is commercial vineyards in the CEVVIN dataset, not every household vine.

title: CEVVIN — Vranac
provenance: Official CEVVIN cultivar and commercial-vineyard profile
summary: Explicitly reports fifteenth place by represented commercial area and a mean commercial-vineyard size of 0.11 ha for Vranac.
notes: The figures describe Serbian commercial records and not the cultivar's wider Montenegro-centred Balkan distribution.

title: CEVVIN — Tamjanika bela
provenance: Official CEVVIN cultivar-group and commercial-vineyard profile
summary: Explicitly reports sixteenth place by represented commercial area and a mean commercial-vineyard size of 0.13 ha for Tamjanika bela.
notes: CEVVIN treats the name as a variable population/group; the statistics should retain that label.

title: CEVVIN — Slankamenka (Grupa Plovina)
provenance: Official CEVVIN grouped cultivar and commercial-vineyard profile
summary: Explicitly reports twenty-second place by represented commercial area and a mean commercial-vineyard size of 0.04 ha for Slankamenka/Grupa Plovina.
notes: The group includes multiple names and should not be silently renamed «Plovdina group».

title: CEVVIN — Tamjanika crna
provenance: Official CEVVIN cultivar-group and commercial-vineyard profile
summary: Explicitly reports thirty-fifth place by represented commercial area and a mean commercial-vineyard size of 0.17 ha for Tamjanika crna.
notes: Identity and origin disputes do not change the fact that this is the category used by the survey.

title: CEVVIN — Kavčina
provenance: Official CEVVIN cultivar profile, values visible in the public search index while direct rendering presented an automated verification page
summary: The indexed official page reports forty-third place by represented commercial area and a mean commercial-vineyard size of 0.12 ha for Kavčina.
notes: The exact values are publicly indexed from the official page; no protected or blurred content was reconstructed.

title: Svet vina — Autohtone i regionalne sorte vinove loze Srbije
provenance: Contemporary 10 August 2019 release notice reproducing CEVVIN's publication announcement
summary: Confirms the catalogue's 2019 release and states that printing was supported through the Ministry's 2018 certification and clonal-selection programme.
notes: The notice does not identify the register observation date, so it cannot turn publication year into a precise survey cutoff.

title: English Wikipedia — Prokupac and Serbian wine
provenance: Requested English Wikipedia corpus and linked Serbian wine article
summary: The Prokupac article describes abundant yields, present high-quality wines and international awards; Serbian wine describes the later socialist industry's quantity-over-quality orientation. Neither reproduces the 1967 manual, its three lists or a period-wide reputation survey.
notes: Useful for context and contrast, not for reconstructing the manual's contents or the authors' causal reasoning.

title: German Wikipedia — Prokupac and Weinbau in Serbien
summary: German Wikipedia calls Prokupac high-yielding and contrasts former Yugoslav mass production with modern private high-quality wines, but contains no Paunović–Daničić bibliography, 1967 grouping or Bagrina consensus evidence.
notes: The historical narrative is later and cannot explain the manual authors' 1967 intent without an explicit bridge source.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia search — Paunović, Daničić, Prokupac and Bagrina classification
summary: No Hungarian Wikipedia article was found that reproduces the 1967 manual's bibliographic record, its three quality groups, the DWWA 2026 result or a historical professional assessment of Prokupac and Bagrina.
notes: Silence does not contradict the primary manual or official award source.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Прокупац and Виноградарство у Србији
provenance: Requested Serbian Wikipedia corpus and linked national viticulture article
summary: Serbian Wikipedia provides basic Prokupac and Serbian viticulture context but does not cite the Paunović–Daničić manual, reproduce the quality groups, explain the cultivar's 1967 placement or document the 2026 Platinum result.
notes: The Serbian corpus does not independently validate the textbook lists or the reputational metaphors.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Виноделие в Сербии and Prokupac searches
summary: Russian Wikipedia supplies general modern Serbian-wine context but no retrievable entry for the 1967 manual's full classification, its authors' rationale, the Bagrina historical generalisation or the precise 2026 award.
notes: No Russian encyclopedic consensus can be inferred for the historical value judgements.

title: Croatian Wikipedia search — 1967 Yugoslav wine-grape classification
summary: No Croatian Wikipedia material was found that reproduces the Paunović–Daničić three-group table or supplies independent evidence for the paragraph's Prokupac and Bagrina interpretations.
notes: Individual Croatian cultivar articles do not reconstruct this Yugoslav manual's table.

title: Paunović and Daničić — Vinarstvo i tehnologija jakih alkoholnih pića (1967 scan)
provenance: Digitized reproduction of the named 1967 Zadružna knjiga manual
summary: Shows the authors, publisher, place, year and the contents heading 'Važnije sorte vinove loze koje se gaje u našoj zemlji', followed by all fourteen group-I, twelve group-II and three group-III entries.
notes: The contents prove placement and omissions but do not state why Prokupac was assigned to group II or measure profession-wide opinion.

title: Knjiga za svakoga — Vinarstvo i tehnologija jakih alkoholnih pića
provenance: Independent antiquarian catalogue transcription of the book metadata and full contents
summary: Independently matches the two authors, Zadružna knjiga, Belgrade, 1967, 473 pages and reproduces the same three group headings and all entries in the same order.
notes: A commercial catalogue is secondary evidence, used only to corroborate the digitized scan.

title: Decanter — DWWA 2026 Platinum winners
provenance: Official Decanter World Wine Awards results
summary: Lists Aleksandrovič Kameničarka Prokupac, Oplenac, Šumadija-Great Morava 2022 among Serbia's 2026 Platinum winners.
notes: The award demonstrates contemporary potential for one wine and vintage; it does not prove why the cultivar was historically ranked lower.

title: CEVVIN — Prokupac
summary: Describes Prokupac as very vigorous and says its must reaches suitable sugar content at reduced yields; it also describes pleasant, refreshing wine and quality improvement with ageing.
notes: Supports the yield–quality tradeoff, not a claim about the motives of the 1967 authors.

title: English Wikipedia — Serbian wine
summary: Uses Kreaca as the ordinary name and Banatski Rizling as an alternative, but gives no Serbian register date, exact parenthetical syntax, Bragina rosie entry or rule connecting synonyms to distribution.
notes: Supports everyday identity only; the current national register controls legal-name wording.

title: German Wikipedia search — Kreaca, Bagrina and Serbian register nomenclature
provenance: Requested German Wikipedia corpus and cultivar searches
summary: German Wikipedia provides general Serbian cultivar context but no retrievable treatment of the current Kreaca or Bragina rosie register entries and no evidence that synonyms prove cultivation geography.
notes: A German page for Portuguese Baga lists Bagrina Crvena as a synonym of a different prime name and cannot substitute for the Serbian register.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia search — Kreaca and Bagrina official names
summary: No Hungarian Wikipedia article was found that reproduces the current Serbian registry forms, distinguishes Kreazer's international status or explains the evidentiary limits of cultivar synonyms.
notes: No conclusion is drawn from absence alone.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Багрина and Виноградарство у Србији
provenance: Requested Serbian Wikipedia corpus and linked cultivar list
summary: Uses the everyday Serbian forms Багрина and Креаца and gives basic cultivation context, but does not reproduce the 2026 state-register main-name/synonym fields or support the claim that a synonym fixes cultivation geography.
notes: Common-language naming can differ from the formal register ordering without contradiction.

title: Russian Wikipedia search — Kreaca, Bagrina and Serbian variety register
summary: The Russian national wine article and cultivar searches do not supply the current Serbian registry spellings, synonym order or a methodology for inferring origin or distribution from synonyms.
notes: The specific nomenclature claim remains dependent on official registers.

title: Croatian Wikipedia search — Kreaca and Bagrina register forms
summary: No Croatian Wikipedia material was found that quotes Serbia's 2026 registered names and synonyms for Kreaca or Bragina rosie or establishes distribution from a synonym.
notes: Neighbouring-country variety lists are separate legal instruments and were not treated as Serbian evidence.

title: Serbian Ministry of Agriculture — Register of Recognised Varieties, 21 July 2026
provenance: Current official register issued by the Plant Protection Directorate's variety-recognition unit
summary: The grape section prints Kreaca (Banatski rizling, Kreacer) and Bragina rosie (Bagrina crvena, Bagrina), with main names outside and synonyms inside parentheses.
notes: The issuing site challenged direct rendering, but its current indexed PDF text exposes both complete entries and the update date.

title: VIVC — KREACA passport
provenance: Julius Kühn Institute Vitis International Variety Catalogue
summary: Uses KREACA as prime name, identifies Serbia in the passport and lists a broad international synonym set including BANATSKI RIZLING, KREACER and KREAZER.
notes: VIVC's broad synonym list does not redefine which aliases the current Serbian national register prints.

title: VIVC — BRAGHINA ROSIE passport
provenance: Julius Kühn Institute Vitis International Variety Catalogue
summary: Uses BRAGHINA ROSIE as prime name and lists BAGRINA CRVENA, BAGRINA KRAJINSKA and other forms as synonyms.
notes: A synonym passport supports name equivalence, not current cultivation geography or a unique centre of origin.

title: Romanian Ministry of Agriculture — ADER 3.1.3 grape-resource list
summary: Lists the cultivar form Braghină roşie in Romanian orthography, independently establishing the linguistic form behind the Serbian register's unaccented Bragina rosie.
notes: Romanian usage does not by itself determine the cultivar's genetic origin or present Serbian distribution.

title: English Wikipedia — Serbian wine
provenance: Requested English Wikipedia corpus and exact-name searches
summary: Gives a short list of major Serbian cultivars and says some rare varieties survive, but does not reproduce CEVVIN's composite rare/minor list, conservation subcategories, thirteen names, source caveat or name etymologies.
notes: The article cannot determine the status or distinct identity of any cultivar in the book paragraph.

title: German Wikipedia — Weinbau in Serbien
provenance: Requested German Wikipedia corpus and exact-name searches
summary: Its varieties section names only established regional and international cultivars; it contains none of the rare-list names or CEVVIN's conservation wording and gives no etymological account.
notes: No conclusion about absence or extinction is drawn from the article's silence.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia search — Serbian rare and endangered grape names
provenance: Requested Hungarian Wikipedia corpus and searches for the exact Serbian names
summary: No Hungarian Wikipedia article was found that reproduces the CEVVIN rare/minor list, assigns the named cultivars to conservation subcategories or explains their names.
notes: Search absence is recorded only as a corpus result and is not evidence that a cultivar is extinct.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Виноградарство у Србији
provenance: Requested Serbian Wikipedia corpus and exact-name searches
summary: Provides general Serbian viticulture history and mainstream varieties but does not reproduce the rare/minor composite category, its individual names, synonym warning or their naming history.
notes: The Serbian-language corpus offers no cultivar-by-cultivar conservation determination for this paragraph.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Виноделие в Сербии
provenance: Requested Russian Wikipedia corpus and exact-name searches
summary: The national wine article contains no equivalent rare-cultivar catalogue, conservation classification, Russian glosses for these names or account of who coined them.
notes: Its silence neither confirms nor refutes the CEVVIN list.

title: Croatian Wikipedia search — Serbian rare grape cultivars
provenance: Requested Croatian Wikipedia corpus and searches for the exact Serbian names
summary: No Croatian Wikipedia material was found that reproduces the CEVVIN list, distinguishes its conservation subgroups, resolves possible synonymy or documents the proposed folk-name origins.
notes: Neighbouring South Slavic lexical transparency is not treated as proof of cultivar identity or history.

title: CEVVIN — Autohtone i regionalne sorte vinove loze Srbije
provenance: Primary institutional catalogue published by Serbia's Centre for Viticulture and Winemaking
summary: The 2019 colophon identifies the publication; page 2 defines a composite rare/minor, non-commercial, individual-vine, endangered and production-vineyard-absent category, lists fifteen names plus others, and warns that some may be synonyms of known autochthonous or regional cultivars.
notes: The PDF lists Volujaraka, Vrna Zelenika and Čauš beli; it gives no Russian translations or social history of the names.

title: CEVVIN — Publikacija: Autohtone i regionalne sorte vinove loze Srbije
summary: Dated 8 August 2019, states that CEVVIN issued the publication as part of its work to promote Serbian autochthonous and regional grape cultivars and links the PDF.
notes: The announcement says the publication covers only some of the most important cultivars; the rare-list taxonomy itself is in the PDF.

title: Milišić — Morfološka i molekularna karakterizacija genotipova vinove loze u Srbiji
provenance: 2024 Serbian doctoral dissertation indexed in the national NARDUS repository
summary: Searchable text treats Serbian grape genetic resources and lists Volujarka, Volovsko oko, Vrna zelenika, Čađavica, Plavetni drenak, Ovči repak, Radovinka and Mirkovača, corroborating the normal Volujarka spelling and continued scholarly treatment of these names.
notes: The repository imposed a human-verification gate, so only indexed text was used; it does not assign every name to one conservation status.

title: Hrvatski jezični portal — čađav and čavka
provenance: Searchable Croatian-language dictionary created by Novi Liber and SRCE
summary: Defines čađav as covered with soot or soot-coloured; the linked čavka entry identifies the jackdaw (Corvus monedula), supporting the literal force of Čađavica and the diminutive Čavčica without establishing cultivar etymology.
notes: Croatian dictionary meanings are lexically relevant across the closely related standard varieties but are not official translations of Serbian cultivar names.

title: Wiktionary — linked Serbo-Croatian component lemmas
provenance: English Wiktionary Serbo-Croatian entries for vol, oko, ovca, rep, vrabac, peršun, šljiva and zlatav
summary: The linked component entries support ox, eye, sheep, tail, sparrow, parsley, plum and golden senses underlying the book's literal Russian glosses.
notes: A collaborative dictionary supports transparent lexical parsing only; it cannot establish when, where or by whom cultivar names were coined.

title: English Wikipedia — Serbian wine
provenance: Requested English Wikipedia corpus and linked cultivar searches
summary: Describes Yugoslavia's 1970s quantity-focused industry, the 1980s–1990s decline and the survival of some rare Serbian varieties, but gives no account of mass local-vineyard clearing, pre-clearing genetic selection programmes or permanent genetic-potential loss.
notes: The article's phrase that some rare varieties survive does not establish that all present autochthonous cultivars survived by chance.

title: German Wikipedia — Weinbau in Serbien
provenance: Requested German Wikipedia corpus and local-cultivar searches
summary: States that international cultivars now dominate Serbian viticulture and gives long historical context for regional grapes, but does not document the CEVVIN clearing narrative, conservation-program chronology or genetic-resource loss.
notes: Its silence cannot date the losses or distinguish planned conservation from chance survival.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia search — Serbian local-grape genetic resources
provenance: Requested Hungarian Wikipedia corpus and searches for Serbian autochthonous cultivars, vineyard clearing and genetic resources
summary: No Hungarian Wikipedia article was found that presents the Serbian mass-clearing claim, dates conservation programmes or attributes current local cultivars to chance survival.
notes: Hungarian cultivar pages such as Kadarka address individual identities and distribution, not Serbia's national conservation history.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Виноградарство у Србији
provenance: Requested Serbian Wikipedia corpus and exact concept searches
summary: Provides a broad cultivar list and links to 2022 genetic-diversity material, but its article text contains no explanation of mass clearing, absent pre-clearing programmes, permanent genetic loss or the preservation status of today's autochthonous cultivars.
notes: The external links show current research interest but do not themselves validate the book's causal compression.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Виноделие в Сербии
provenance: Requested Russian Wikipedia corpus and exact concept searches
summary: Lists several cultivated Serbian grapes but contains no autochthonous-resource history, mass-clearing chronology, selection-program evidence or genetic-loss assessment.
notes: The article cannot support either the institutional loss claim or the final chance-survival metaphor.

title: Croatian Wikipedia search — Serbian autochthonous-grape conservation
provenance: Requested Croatian Wikipedia corpus and searches for Serbian local cultivars, clearing and genetic resources
summary: No Croatian Wikipedia article was found that reproduces CEVVIN's national conservation account or resolves whether surviving Serbian local cultivars were preserved deliberately or by chance.
notes: Croatian material about individual regional cultivars is not a substitute for Serbian conservation-program evidence.

title: CEVVIN — Autohtone i regionalne sorte vinove loze Srbije
provenance: Primary 2019 institutional catalogue by Serbia's Centre for Viticulture and Winemaking
summary: Page 1 calls mass grubbing-up and deterioration of local-variety vineyards in a previous period a basic problem, says special programmes had not saved those vineyards and selected the best material before clearing, and describes the lost areas as a permanent loss of grapevine genetic potential; it then presents an active CEVVIN programme.
notes: The source says 'previous period' rather than a dated set of decades and does not call clearing the single cause of all present-day scarcity.

title: CEVVIN — Genetički resursi
provenance: Current official genetic-resources page of Serbia's Centre for Viticulture and Winemaking
summary: Says old traditional-variety vineyards disappear through abandonment and economically motivated clearing; calls each unexamined and cleared local-variety vineyard irreplaceable, then details inventory, field evaluation, GIS, databases, propagation, collection-vineyard preservation and clonal selection.
notes: The simultaneous loss and conservation activity contradicts a simple all-or-nothing account of unprotected chance survival.

title: Jakšić et al. — Classification of Sustainability Potential of Genetic Resources of Local Grapevine Varieties in Serbia
provenance: 2024 original article in Matica Srpska Journal of Natural Sciences, DOI 10.2298/ZMSPN2446091J
summary: Reports 31 local wine varieties among 224 commercial grapevine varieties, repeats the mass-grubbing, deterioration, missing special-programme and permanent-loss account, but also models 10,402 local-variety vineyards, separates endangered from sustainable holdings and notes that some local cultivars are expanding while others approach disappearance.
notes: The paper supports the institutional loss diagnosis but not a claim that every local cultivar survives only by chance or that none was preserved.

title: Tello et al. — The genetic characterization of grapevines prospected in old Serbian vineyards
provenance: 2024 original research article in Frontiers in Plant Science
summary: Documents older phylloxera losses and replacement with foreign cultivars, then analyses 138 vines from extant old Serbian vineyards; the sample also includes some isolated vines that survived clearing in meadows and forest edges, revealing both deliberate prospection and a limited chance-survivor pathway.
notes: The study says Serbia preserves a high number of local varieties and does not generalize isolated survivors to the entire present assortment.

title: Sivčev, Ranković-Vasić and Radovanović — Clone selection in old vineyards of southeastern and eastern Serbia
provenance: 2011 original research article in Genetika, DOI 10.2298/GENSR1103465S
summary: Reports that clone and sanitary selection to preserve old-vineyard varieties began in southeastern Serbia in 2006, examined 1,048 vines and selected candidates including Prokupac; work expanded to eastern Serbia in 2008.
notes: This does not disprove CEVVIN's claim that many vineyards were lost without prior programmes, but it rules out reading 'programmes did not exist' as an unlimited statement about all recent Serbian work.

title: Pržić and Marković — Clonal selection and valorisation of autochthonous grape cultivars in Serbia
summary: Calls Serbia's autochthonous assortment reduced to a few cultivars and reports first varietal-selection results for Smederevka and Prokupac, with four and twelve selected clones respectively.
notes: The narrow first-selection statement concerns these two cultivars and cannot establish that no earlier preservation project existed for any Serbian grape.

title: English Wikipedia — Kadarka, Prokupac, Tamjanika, Vranac and Serbian wine
provenance: Requested English Wikipedia corpus and linked cultivar searches
summary: Presents Prokupac as Serbian, Vranac as Montenegrin, white Tamjanika as belonging to the Muscat family and Kadarka origin as disputed between a Shkodër-area and Hungarian hypothesis; it neither documents the CEVVIN publication's exact status nor Petrović's full position, Bagrina classification or the methodological limits of the 2024 Serbian genetic study.
notes: The Kadarka page repeats disputed origin narratives and should not be treated as a resolution of birthplace; its Tamjanika wording does not support a specifically French derivation.

title: German Wikipedia — Weinbau in Serbien
provenance: Requested German Wikipedia corpus and linked Prokupac and Vranac articles
summary: Groups Prokupac, Kadarka, Tamjanika, Smederevka, Vranac and Krstač as regional Serbian-wine cultivars; the linked Prokupac article calls that cultivar Serbian and the linked Vranac article gives a wider southern-Yugoslav distribution, but the corpus does not reproduce CEVVIN's internal status distinctions or Petrović's claims.
notes: The general wine article uses regional and autochthonous language loosely and cannot adjudicate Bagrina, Tamjanika identity or origin methodology.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Kadarka
summary: States that Kadarka's origin is uncertain, with Asia Minor and Albania proposed, and that it reached Hungary from the Balkans, probably through Serbian mediation, in the eighteenth century; it provides no evidence for the other cultivars, CEVVIN source status or Petrović attribution.
notes: The article distinguishes uncertain origin from later Hungarian distribution, which cautions against compressing Montenegro and Hungary into one settled birthplace claim.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Прокупац and linked cultivar searches
summary: The Prokupac article treats the cultivar in Serbian viticultural context, while the Tamjanika article labels it Serbian without resolving Muscat identity or origin; no Serbian Wikipedia page found in the selected searches supplies Petrović's nuanced interview position, the CEVVIN category wording or the genetic-study caveats.
notes: The Serbian Tamjanika infobox is weaker than the primary genetic and VIVC evidence and is recorded as a corpus result, not adopted as consensus.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Виноделие в Сербии and Кадарка
provenance: Requested Russian Wikipedia corpus and linked cultivar search
summary: Lists Prokupac, Vranac, Tamjanika and Kadarka among Serbian-grown cultivars and calls Tamjanika a local mutation of white Muscat; the separate Kadarka page records broad Balkan and Hungarian distribution but no origin analysis. The corpus does not support the exact professor attribution or the claimed French derivation.
notes: The unsourced mutation wording is not sufficient to override CEVVIN's non-prejudgment or the 2024 genetic identification of sampled Tamjanika Ćilibarka as Muscat à Petits Grains.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Kadarka and Vranac
provenance: Requested Croatian Wikipedia corpus and linked cultivar search
summary: Presents Kadarka as a Pannonian cultivar with competing Lake Skadar and Hungarian origin theories; the Vranac article describes it as autochthonous across several Balkan countries and especially important in Montenegro, while the corpus is silent on Petrović, Bagrina, Kavčina and the genetic-network methodology.
notes: The Croatian pages demonstrate the instability of national-origin labels rather than establishing a single origin centre.

title: CEVVIN — Autohtone i regionalne sorte vinove loze Srbije
provenance: Primary 2019 institutional publication by Serbia's Centre for Viticulture and Winemaking
summary: Its commercial-vineyard list combines autochthonous and regional cultivars. It calls Tamjanika crna regional and international, Kavčina Central European and grown in Austria and Germany, Vranac a cultivar of Montenegro, and Prokupac the most important Serbian autochthonous cultivar; for the white Tamjanika group it explicitly avoids prejudging origin.
notes: This expert publication is not the statutory Serbian variety register; its mixed umbrella is central to interpreting the word 'local'.

title: CEVVIN — O Centru
summary: States that the Republic of Serbia founded CEVVIN, that it is a national expert and research institution, and that it performs vineyard-register and other professional work for ministries.
notes: Institutional authority does not turn every CEVVIN publication into a statutory register or legal classification instrument.

title: Danas — Vinska mapa Srbije: Profesor Aleksandar Petrović otkriva gde nastaju najbolji rizlinzi, šardonei i prokupci
provenance: 9 April 2025 interview reproduced from vinologija.rs; identifies Petrović as an associate professor at the University of Belgrade Faculty of Agriculture
summary: Petrović calls Prokupac the only certain Serbian original cultivar but immediately allows Začinak and possibly Kreaca; says Bagrina is considered Romanian; treats black Tamjanika as uncertain and identifies white Tamjanika with Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains and its Frontignan and Austrian names while leaving origin uncertain. Kadarka is not discussed.
notes: The article supports reporting his view, not promoting every view to genetic or catalogue consensus; Muscat de Frontignan is presented as an alternative name, not a French ancestor.

title: NIN — Gde je Srbija na vinskoj karti Evrope
summary: Quotes Petrović treating Kadarka as a name derived from Skadarka while noting a Hungarian claim, and later calls Začinak almost certainly Serbia's second autochthonous cultivar after Prokupac.
notes: The Kadarka passage does not itself say Montenegro; that geography enters through the separate Lake Skadar origin hypothesis.

title: VIVC passport — KADARKA KEK
provenance: Scientifically curated Vitis International Variety Catalogue passport
summary: Assigns KADARKA KEK VIVC 5898 to Hungary and records its international identity and synonyms.
notes: A catalogue country assignment is relevant evidence but does not by itself settle competing historical birthplace and transmission hypotheses.

title: VIVC passport — BRAGHINA ROSIE
provenance: Scientifically curated Vitis International Variety Catalogue passport
summary: Uses BRAGHINA ROSIE as the prime name for VIVC 1644 and assigns the cultivar to Serbia.
notes: This conflicts with the expert interview's Romanian attribution and requires the book to label that statement as Petrović's view rather than an uncontested fact.

title: VIVC passport — MUSCAT A PETITS GRAINS BLANCS
provenance: Scientifically curated Vitis International Variety Catalogue passport
summary: Records MUSCAT A PETITS GRAINS BLANCS as VIVC 8193 and assigns its country or region of origin to Greece.
notes: The French place-name synonym Frontignan cannot be converted into a French origin or parentage claim without separate evidence.

title: VIVC passport — PROKUPAC
provenance: Scientifically curated Vitis International Variety Catalogue passport
summary: Records PROKUPAC as VIVC 9734 with Serbia as country or region of origin.
notes: This supports Prokupac's Serbian status but does not prove that it is the only Serbian autochthonous cultivar.

title: Tello et al. — The genetic characterization of grapevines prospected in old Serbian vineyards reveals multiple relationships between traditional varieties of the Balkans
provenance: 2024 original research in Frontiers in Plant Science, DOI 10.3389/fpls.2024.1391679
summary: Profiles 138 vines and finds 59 genetic profiles, most in a complex cross-border Balkan pedigree network. It treats Prokupac, Začinak and Braghina Rosie as Serbian in its VIVC-derived table, identifies sampled Tamjanika Ćilibarka as Muscat à Petits Grains, and expressly states that the analyses were not designed to determine cultivation duration in Serbia.
notes: The study can support pedigree and long regional presence in some cases, but it cautions against deriving an exact cultivation timeline; its network does not alone locate a unique birthplace for every cultivar.

title: Jakšić et al. — Classification of Sustainability Potential of Local Grapevine Variety Vineyards in Serbia
provenance: 2024 original research in Matica Srpska Journal for Natural Sciences, DOI 10.2298/ZMSPN2446091J
summary: Explicitly avoids literal name-and-origin taxonomy and defines 'local grapevine varieties' for the paper as autochthonous, regional and old cultivars grown in Serbia for a long time, then lists 31 such wine cultivars.
notes: The definition is a transparent research convention; it does not establish a centuries-long Serbian history or local breeding origin for each listed cultivar.

title: PlantGrape — Kadarka
provenance: French official grape-cultivar catalogue maintained from INRAE and Institut Agro Montpellier resources
summary: Describes Kadarka as originally cultivated in Hungary and the Balkans and possibly of Ottoman origin, and separately records its regulatory names and registrations in European catalogues.
notes: This wider formulation supports caution toward a unique Montenegro-or-Hungary birthplace and separates traditional cultivation area from regulatory registration.

title: English Wikipedia — Serbian wine
summary: Describes Yugoslavia's production peak in the 1970s, quantity-oriented socialism and mass production in large combines such as Navip and Rubin, and lists both international and local cultivars; it gives neither the current 224-cultivar count nor planted-area proof of Western European dominance or supplier-variety control.
notes: The article's current vineyard-area figure is obsolete and was not used; its historical paragraph is treated as secondary context, not as proof of the full causal chain.

title: German Wikipedia — Weinbau in Serbien
summary: Names regional cultivars and international partners such as Riesling, Pinot noir, Gamay, Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon, but supplies no current cultivar count or area shares and does not cover the socialist combine history, supplier relations or the proposed 1970s causation.
notes: The article's broad regional-versus-international grouping cannot establish comparative planted-area dominance.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia search — Serbian cultivar structure and socialist wine combines
summary: No Hungarian Wikipedia article was found that reports Serbia's current cultivar count or planted-area structure, reconstructs the role of Serbian wine combines in the 1970s or documents control of supplier cultivar choices.
notes: The Szerém wine-region and Kadarka articles provide separate regional history but not evidence for this national Serbian paragraph.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Виноградарство у Србији
summary: Provides a long unranked list of Serbian-grown cultivars including Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay and numerous local varieties; its history ends with early twentieth-century developments and does not quantify current dominance or examine socialist combines and their suppliers.
notes: An unranked list proves cultivation only, not dominance by cultivar origin, count or area.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Виноделие в Сербии
summary: Lists international and local cultivars grown in Serbia but supplies no total cultivar count, planted-area shares or 1970s combine history and no evidence that wineries prescribed suppliers' varieties.
notes: The page was last edited in 2022 and its list is not a statistical distribution.

title: Croatian Wikipedia search — Serbian cultivar structure and Yugoslav wine combines
summary: No Croatian Wikipedia material was found that reports Serbia's cultivar total or area structure or establishes the paragraph's causal sequence from 1970s combines to suppliers' cultivar choices.
notes: General Croatian wine and cultivar pages do not substitute for Serbian national statistics or combine records.

title: Jakšić et al. — Classification of Sustainability Potential of Local Grapevine Variety Vineyards in Serbia
provenance: 2024 original research in Matica Srpska Journal for Natural Sciences, DOI 10.2298/ZMSPN2446091J
summary: Reports 224 cultivars currently used for commercial grape and wine production in Serbia, of which 31 wine cultivars, or 13.84%, are grouped as local; it defines local as an umbrella for autochthonous, regional and long-grown old cultivars.
notes: The share is a share of cultivar names, not planted hectares, and cannot alone prove international area dominance or the relative interest of the groups.

title: CEVVIN — Анализа сектора производње и прераде грожђа и производње вина
provenance: Primary institutional sector study dated 31 March 2019, based on Serbian statistical, vineyard, winery and planting-material registers
summary: Identifies Graševina, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay and Riesling as the five leading international cultivars by registered area, while explicitly treating Graševina as regional but grouping it internationally for that analysis; it also finds recent nursery production dominated by international cultivars and notes the decline of former large social wineries.
notes: Its area data are dated 2019 and its analytical origin categories differ from the 2024 paper's broad local umbrella, so dates, register scope and category rules must be stated.

title: New Europe Wine Guide — Serbia 2026
provenance: 2026 specialist wine guide citing the 2024 Serbian Vineyard Register
summary: Lists the 2024 register's main varieties as Grašac 11%, Chardonnay 9%, Riesling 6%, Sauvignon Blanc 5%, Merlot 11%, Cabernet Sauvignon 9% and Prokupac 5%; the five named international cultivars sum to 40% of total plantings.
notes: The guide does not reproduce the complete register table, so the listed leaders corroborate importance but are not by themselves a full origin-group total.

title: Marković and Pržić — Serbian Viticulture from the 19th Century to the Present Day
provenance: 2022 historical review in Annals of the University of Craiova, Agriculture, Montanology, Cadastre Series 52/1
summary: Dates intensive vineyard planting to 1959-1970, links it to mechanization and new cultivars, documents large state wineries and intensive plantings of Pinot, Cabernet, Merlot, Riesling, Sauvignon and other cultivars, and gives the land split around 1970 as 106,000 ha individual versus 10,500 ha state sector.
notes: It supports strong state influence and international planting but not the claim that state wineries dictated the varieties planted by private suppliers.

title: Netherlands agricultural network — The vineyard of the Balkans: Wine in Serbia
provenance: 2020 briefing on the Dutch Ministry of Agriculture international network, drawing on Serbian official statistics and registers
summary: Describes large collectivized state-owned companies after the world wars, Yugoslavia's 1970s production peak and the later practice of large wineries buying grapes from small producers; it separately records the continuing category of growers who sell grapes to wine companies.
notes: It does not say those companies prescribed supplier cultivars, and its 135,000 ha figure is the national vineyard total in 1955 rather than a demonstrated company-owned total.

title: Jancis Robinson — Made in Serbia
provenance: 2017 specialist field report by Caroline Gilby MW
summary: Reports that state cooperatives replaced much Prokupac with international cultivars after it was judged unsuitable by the 1960s, describes former state-winery giants and documents the then leading registered variety shares and successful international-cultivar wines.
notes: This moves part of the causal chronology earlier than the book's 1970s formulation and does not quantify who selected varieties in supplier-owned vineyards.

title: Association of Winemakers and Winegrowers of Serbia — I'm picking grapes, I'm choosing tamjanika
provenance: National producer-association page using Serbian Vineyard Register data
summary: States that Serbian grape and wine production is mainly focused on international cultivars and that indigenous, local and newly created cultivars account for about 8% within its cited 5,763.43 ha analysed register scope; it frames local cultivars as carriers of authenticity and local character.
notes: The page gives no publication date and uses a narrower category and register subset than the 2024 local-cultivar paper; its regional-character language remains advocacy, not an objective comparison of interest.

title: Osservatorio Balcani Caucaso Transeuropa — Yugoslav wine: a story of crisis and renovation
provenance: 10 August 2026 historical feature based on sector interviews and OIV and Oxford Companion context
summary: Describes centralized, quota-oriented Yugoslav industrial plants buying grapes from individual growers and the production peak of the 1970s, but does not state that Serbian combines selected or prescribed the suppliers' cultivars.
notes: The feature concerns Yugoslavia broadly and cannot by itself establish a Serbia-specific supplier-planting rule.

title: English Wikipedia — Welschriesling
summary: Maps Welschriesling to Grašac, Graševina, Riesling Italico and Italian Riesling, explicitly distinguishes it from Rhine Riesling and describes wide Central and Southeastern European distribution. It gives no current regional share, revival chronology, Serbian analytical range or detailed sensory profile.
notes: Its claim that the cultivar is Serbia's most planted by total area relies on older data and is not used against the end-2025 commercial register.

title: German Wikipedia — Welschriesling
summary: Confirms synonymy and no relationship to Rhine Riesling; for young dry wine it gives pale green-yellow colour, light structure, floral-fruity aroma dominated by green apple and a brisk fresh palate, while also documenting sweet and sparkling styles. It does not establish Serbian regional shares, revival or analytical ranges.
notes: The generic Austrian-centred profile is useful for style boundaries but cannot be treated as a representative tasting of Serbian Grašac.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Olaszrizling
summary: Uses Olaszrizling for the same widely grown Central European cultivar and supplies Hungarian history and general wine context, but no Serbia-specific regional proportion, revival evidence, product chemistry or source-based almond distinction.
notes: Hungarian material helps establish international distribution and nomenclature, not current Serbian denominators.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Грашевина
summary: Identifies Graševina/Italian Riesling as a Central European white cultivar and distinguishes it from Rhine Riesling. The short page does not substantiate the two regional majority claim, modern revival, exact sensory wording or alcohol and acidity ranges.
notes: Local language does not compensate for absent dates, denominators and product-level evidence.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Вельшрислинг
summary: Confirms the multinational synonym set, uncertain origin and distinction from Rhine Riesling, with general cultivation and wine-style context. It provides no current Serbian regional-share evidence, revival chronology or analytical specification.
notes: The article substantially follows shared international material and is not counted as an independent Serbian statistical line.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Graševina
summary: Identifies Graševina with Welschriesling/Italian Riesling and describes a usually dry, fresh, slightly bitter regional wine whose aroma varies with site. It does not prove Serbia's two regional majorities, current revival, precise alcohol or acidity range, or the assertion that almond wording lacks sources.
notes: The page has weak legacy sourcing and is used cautiously for the neighbouring regional tradition rather than Serbian statistics.

title: GuildSomm — GROW: A Grape with an Identity Crisis
provenance: Current specialist synthesis by Caroline Gilby MW drawing on genetic and aroma research and regional reporting
summary: Documents the Grašac name revival and Serbia's quality-producer movement, distinguishes the cultivar from Rhine Riesling, and describes light fruity wines with lemon, grapefruit, green apple, white flowers and slight almond bitterness. It stresses wide style variation and says the cultivar was formerly considered neutral and ordinary.
notes: Its Serbian area estimate uses older 13% register data and is not used for the current regional or national rank.

title: Polyphenolic profile, antioxidant and neuroprotective potency of grape juices and wines from Fruška Gora region
provenance: 2017 peer-reviewed article in International Journal of Food Properties
summary: States in its background that Italian Riesling occupied more than half of Fruška Gora vineyards and identifies its Graševina/Olaszrizling synonyms.
notes: The share comes from earlier regional literature rather than the authors' own vineyard inventory; no current official regional breakdown was found.

title: Vinski Vodič — Vršački vinogradi
summary: Reports Italian Riesling at more than 50% of the assortment of Vršački vinogradi, the large enterprise, but does not give the cultivar's share of every vineyard parcel in the wider Vršac wine district.
notes: The company assortment cannot be generalized to the whole region without a dated vineyard-register table.

title: The Buyer — How Central Europe's Grašac white wine variety has been reborn
provenance: 21 November 2025 specialist feature by Ian Bancroft with named Serbian and regional wine professionals
summary: Directly documents the Serbian return to the Grašac name, increased sales, new plot selection and stainless, lees, acacia, barrel, sparkling, sweet and orange experimentation. It gives delicate green-apple, pear and citrus aromas and treats the process as reputational and stylistic revival.
notes: Several causal details are interview testimony and do not constitute a controlled market study; they nevertheless define what the reported revival means.

title: SerbianWine.rs — Grašac Beli: The Serbian White Grape Guide
provenance: User-requested current Serbian public wine guide with cited genetics and tourism sources
summary: Calls Grašac the historic Serbian name of internationally distributed Welschriesling, not a uniquely Serbian genotype, and locates its modern identity on Fruška Gora. Typical dry examples show green or yellow apple, pear, citrus, herbs, hay and a gently bitter finish, while the guide stresses versatility rather than one dramatic aroma.
notes: The page is recent secondary guidance and does not supply a representative chemical dataset or a source for the exact collective oenologist quotation.

title: Erdevik Winery — Geronimo Grašac 2021
summary: Lists a dry 100% Graschatz from Fruška Gora at 12.5% alcohol, 6.14 g/L total acid, 1.80 g/L residual sugar and pH 3.27, with lime, orange peel, Golden Delicious, herbs and a citrus finish.
notes: One vintage supports the common range but cannot define the entire cultivar.

title: Vinarija Verkat — Grašac Beli 2023
provenance: Official winery technical and sensory specification
summary: Gives light yellow-green colour, citrus with dried-herb and green notes, 13% alcohol, 0.5 g/L residual sugar, 6.5 g/L acids and pH 3.15 for a current dry stainless-steel Grašac.
notes: The product fits the book's numerical range but its aromatic profile is not dominated by green apple.

title: Imperator — Cargraš 2024
summary: Lists dry 100% Grašac at 13.5% alcohol, 1.0 g/L residual sugar, pH 3.35 and 5.4 g/L total acidity.
notes: Shows why 11–13% cannot serve as a complete current varietal range even though 5–7 g/L fits this wine.

title: Vino.rs — Vinum grašac horizontally and vertically
provenance: Independent specialist report of a multi-vintage, multi-style Vinum tasting with winemaker data
summary: Records gold-to-green colour, peach, apple and grapefruit in still Grašac, Dina sparkling at just under 12% alcohol and 7.2 g/L acidity, and barrel-aged Grašac 26A 2020 at 14.5% alcohol and 5.8 g/L acidity.
notes: The report demonstrates diversity within one producer; the chemistry is named-wine evidence rather than a population distribution.

title: Vina Srbije — Verkat Grašac Beli 4.0 2021
provenance: Serbian product catalogue reproducing a named wine's technical specification
summary: Lists 13% alcohol, 7.5 g/L acidity and pH 3.10, with citrus, banana, dry herbs and nut notes for a selected low-yield Grašac.
notes: Secondary product data should be checked against the producer if used in the book; it is sufficient here to show that 7 g/L is not a hard upper limit.

title: Serbian wine-product regulation — total acidity expressed as tartaric acid
provenance: Consolidated text of Serbian Official Gazette provisions 26/2015, 93/2015, 41/2017 and 84/2018
summary: Uses the legal analytical formulation 'total acidity, expressed as tartaric acid' in grams per litre, confirming that the book's stated reference acid and unit follow Serbian convention.
notes: The regulation establishes the reporting convention and minima, not a Grašac-specific 5–7 g/L range.

title: Uncorking the Wine World — Vojvodina Wine Show 2019
provenance: Independent 2019 field report by wine writer and international competition judge Ivana Simjanovska
summary: Reports a vertical tasting of Fruškogorski Vinogradi Grašac 2017, 2015 and 2012; the 2012 wine showed marzipan and almond aromas plus marzipan flavour on the palate.
notes: This is a tasting note for one aged wine, not proof that every young Grašac has almond bitterness; it directly disproves the claim that sources only use generic bitterness.

title: Ministry of Agriculture — Green Book 2025, Book II
provenance: Official Serbian Ministry report based on the Vineyard Register, chart 46
summary: At end-2025 Chardonnay accounts for 9% of vineyards intended predominantly for commercial grape production, ranking third overall after Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon and first among white cultivars.
notes: The register scope does not include every household, abandoned or unregistered vine, and national rank does not make the word «everywhere» literal.

title: Decanter — Explore the Serbia wine region
provenance: Caroline Gilby MW guide produced with Serbian tourism and wine-sector partners
summary: Calls international grapes important to Serbia's transformed modern wine scene and says Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot do particularly well, citing multiple DWWA Gold and Platinum results; it treats both Vojvodina and central Serbia as major zones.
notes: The page is sponsored and qualitative; the Ministry register supplies the independent quantitative control.

title: DWWA 2026 wine search — Serbia
provenance: Official Decanter World Wine Awards results database
summary: The Serbia result set contains seven 95-point Gold wines. Three are Chardonnay wines: Tarpoš Chardonnay Extra Brut 2021, Zvonko Bogdan Chardonnay 2022 and Zvonko Bogdan Éclater Blanc de Blancs Brut Nature 2018.
notes: The dynamic interface is the primary award index; exact composition of Éclater is confirmed separately by its producer.

title: Tanjug — Srpska vina osvojila tri platinaste medalje na DWWA 2026
provenance: Tanjug report reproducing the Serbian Chamber of Commerce announcement, 19 June 2026
summary: Reports seven Serbian Golds and lists all seven, including the three Chardonnay wines, and separately identifies Deurić La Rem Chardonnay 2023 among three Serbian Platinum wines with 97 points.
notes: The Gold list exactly matches specialist reporting and the official searchable results; the Platinum identity also matches Decanter's official article.

title: Zvonko Bogdan Winery — Eclater 2018
summary: Identifies Éclater harvest 2018 as Chardonnay made by the traditional bottle-fermentation method, with 46 months on lees and zero dosage.
notes: This resolves the otherwise non-obvious cultivar behind the Blanc de Blancs label; the current page intermittently returns a gateway error but remains indexed.

title: Decanter — DWWA 2026 Platinum winners
provenance: Official Decanter World Wine Awards results article
summary: The full Serbia section lists Deurić, La Rem Chardonnay, Fruška Gora, Srem 2023 among the 2026 Platinum winners; the article explains that Platinum wines are retasted Gold winners and occupy the 97-point tier.
notes: The result belongs to the named wine and vintage, not to all Deurić Chardonnay or the cultivar as a whole.

title: New Europe Wine Guide — Serbia 2026
provenance: Beth Willard's current multi-region tasting guide covering 268 named wines from 62 producers over three days in December 2025
summary: Documents Chardonnay across Vojvodina and central Serbia. Northern examples range from elegant, saline La Rem and bright-acid Rajić to full 14.5% Grumen and broad creamy Picus; Šumadija ranges from bright 12% Trijumf sparkling and precise Camille 2024 to opulent Aberdar and very ripe 14.5% Savić 2022.
notes: The guide does not state that the tasting was blind and is not a controlled regional experiment; style and ripeness also reflect vintage, harvest decisions, oak, lees and malolactic choices.

title: English Wikipedia — Chardonnay
summary: Describes Chardonnay as globally planted and highly malleable, with styles shaped by climate, terroir, oak and malolactic fermentation; cooler conditions often give lighter, higher-acid apple and pear profiles, while warmer conditions shift toward peach, melon and tropical fruit.
notes: The article provides the conceptual climate-style model but no Serbian 2026 award list or north-versus-Šumadija comparative sample.

title: German Wikipedia — Chardonnay
summary: Treats Chardonnay as a globally important cultivar capable of very different wines depending on climate and terroir, while also emphasizing ripeness, body and the major influence of oak maturation.
notes: It contains no Serbia-specific 2026 awards or north-central sensory comparison.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Chardonnay (szőlőfajta)
summary: Identifies Chardonnay as a worldwide cultivar grown in wine-producing countries across the world.
notes: No Serbian area share, DWWA award arithmetic or regional style comparison is present.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Шардоне
summary: Defines Chardonnay as a highly sought-after white cultivar of Burgundian origin, now grown worldwide, adaptable to different soils and associated generally with apple, melon and pineapple.
notes: The page does not quantify Serbian plantings, record DWWA 2026 results or distinguish northern and Šumadija wines.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Шардоне
summary: Classifies Chardonnay as a Burgundian technical white cultivar cultivated in all wine-producing countries and one of the principal international varieties.
notes: It supplies no current Serbian statistics, DWWA arithmetic, Deurić result or regional sensory comparison.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Chardonnay
summary: Presents Chardonnay as one of the world's best-known wine grapes and summarizes its Pinot × Gouais Blanc parentage.
notes: The article does not support the Serbian rank, 2026 awards or the proposed regional style binary.

title: Vino & Fino — Tri platine i sedam zlata za Srbiju na Dekanteru
summary: Prints all three Serbian Platinum and all seven Gold results: the Gold list contains Tarpoš Chardonnay Extra Brut 2021, Zvonko Bogdan Chardonnay 2022 and Éclater 2018, while La Rem Chardonnay 2023 is Platinum with 97 points.
notes: The result list agrees with Tanjug/Chamber reporting and the official Decanter sources.

title: New Europe Wine Guide — Serbia 2026
provenance: Beth Willard's guide based on 268 named wines from 62 Serbian producers tasted over three days in December 2025
summary: Reports Sauvignon Blanc at 5% of Serbia's end-2024 registered commercial vineyard area and reviews it across several regions. SoviNoa Fumé Blanc 2023 receives 96 and Top White Wine; its note combines lime, nettle, florals and smoky oak. Other northern, Šumadija and southern examples repeatedly mix gooseberry, grass or nettle with peach, pineapple, citrus, apple or tropical fruit.
notes: The guide does not call its tasting a competition or print a Top Sauvignon Blanc category; SoviNoa Fumé Blanc is nevertheless the highest-scoring Sauvignon Blanc in its results.

title: Decanter — International Sauvignon Blanc Day: Award-winning wines to celebrate
provenance: Official Decanter World Wine Awards editorial and result record
summary: Identifies Matijašević SoviNoa Fumé Blanc 2021 as a Serbian Sauvignon Blanc and DWWA 2023 Gold with 95 points, describing peach, gooseberry, grapefruit, citrus, oak, stone fruit and lemongrass together.
notes: This official Decanter result concerns vintage 2021 and 95 points, not the 2023 wine's 96-point New Europe score.

title: Matijašević Vinogradi — SoviNoa Fumé Blanc
summary: Identifies the wine as selected Sauvignon Blanc matured in French oak and describes tropical fruit, ripe peach, citrus, spicy and dried herbs, oak and a long finish.
notes: Producer descriptions are useful for identity and method but do not independently establish a national best-wine rank; the page combines a current product record with earlier award history.

title: Wines of Serbia — Matijašević Vinogradi
provenance: Official Wines of Serbia winery directory
summary: Places Matijašević Vinogradi in Orašac in the Šumadija wine region and lists Sauvignon Blanc among its varieties and SoviNoa and SoviNoa Fumé among its wines.
notes: Directory evidence establishes location and portfolio, not the comparative rank or source of the 96-point score.

title: Wines of Serbia — Vinarija Frug
provenance: Official Wines of Serbia winery directory
summary: Places Vinarija Frug in the Fruška Gora/Srem region and lists Sauvignon Blanc, corroborating current commercial presence in the northern region named by the book.
notes: The directory does not by itself establish a uniform regional flavour profile; wine-level tasting evidence is required for that comparison.

title: Atelje Šapat — Atila Sauvignon Blanc
provenance: Official Fruška Gora producer product specification
summary: Describes a 100% Sauvignon Blanc from the north with lime, gooseberry, vineyard peach, lemongrass, elder, green apple, minerality and fresh acidity, directly showing green, floral and ripe-fruit descriptors in the same regional wine.
notes: One wine cannot define Fruška Gora as a whole, but it contradicts a simple north-green versus south-yellow exclusivity.

title: wein.plus glossary — Sauvignon Blanc
summary: Summarizes the cultivar's broad aromatic range, including grass, herbs, gooseberry and green fruit alongside grapefruit and riper fruit expressions, with climate and ripeness affecting style.
notes: General cultivar evidence supports the plausibility of the descriptors but cannot prove a Serbian regional boundary.

title: Vino.rs — Srpska vina u debelom zlatu
provenance: Serbian specialist report on the New Europe Wine Guide – Serbia 2026
summary: Attributes SoviNoa Fumé Blanc 2023's 96 points to Beth Willard's New Europe Wine Guide and reports the category Top White Wine. It notes Willard's Decanter/DWWA role but does not present the score as a Decanter result.
notes: The assessor's professional connection to Decanter does not turn an independently published guide score into a Decanter score.

title: English Wikipedia — Sauvignon blanc
summary: Describes a global cultivar whose wines may show grassy, bell-pepper, nettle, elderflower and tropical-fruit characters depending on climate and ripeness.
notes: It contains no Matijašević wine, 96-point score, New Europe category or controlled Serbian regional comparison.

title: German Wikipedia — Sauvignon Blanc
summary: Lists gooseberry and green freshly mown grass among characteristic Sauvignon Blanc aromas and records the variety's international distribution, including Serbia.
notes: No Serbian regional split, producer ranking, guide category or Decanter attribution is provided.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Sauvignon blanc
summary: Provides only broad international and aromatic cultivar context for Sauvignon Blanc.
notes: It does not support the named Serbian regions, wine, score, assessor or category.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Совињон блан
summary: Describes Sauvignon Blanc as a dry refreshing wine associated generally with grass, ripe melon, passion fruit and fig.
notes: It supplies no regional Serbian evidence or Matijašević/New Europe/Decanter result.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Совиньон-блан
summary: Lists gooseberry and freshly cut grass, explains a cooler-to-warmer shift toward tropical fruit and includes Serbia among producing countries.
notes: The article does not prove that Serbian southern wines replace rather than combine green notes, nor does it cover SoviNoa's score.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Sauvignon
summary: Provides general Sauvignon descriptors including green apple, grapefruit, asparagus and wet grass.
notes: It contains no Serbian regional comparison, Matijašević identity, score source or guide category.

title: Vinarija Džervin — current wines and Knjaževac vineyards
summary: Declares a varietal Knjaževac Rhine Riesling 2021, basic Dubravka 2024 as 70% Italian Riesling plus 30% Rhine Riesling, and Dubravka Gold 2024 as 50% Italian Riesling plus 50% Sauvignon Blanc; the estate vineyards lie near Knjaževac at 250–330 metres.
notes: The three product cards distinguish Rhine from Italian Riesling and directly contradict putting Rhine Riesling into the current Gold bottling.

title: Tourism Organisation of Negotin — Wineries
provenance: Official local tourism organisation winery directory
summary: Lists Rhine Riesling among wines or varieties of producers in the Negotin wine area, establishing local presence without a comparative quality ranking against every other white cultivar.
notes: A promotional directory can show current production but cannot by itself establish the cultivar as the region's objectively best white.

title: Wines of Serbia — Vinarija Imperator (& Salaxia)
provenance: Official Wines of Serbia winery directory
summary: Places Imperator's 9.3-hectare vineyard near Erdevik on Fruška Gora and explicitly lists Rhine Riesling among its planted varieties.
notes: One producer proves current presence, not a complete regional area or quality ranking.

title: CEVVIN/Ministry — Rejonizacija vinogradarskih geografskih proizvodnih područja Srbije
provenance: Official national zoning study underlying Serbian viticultural regulation
summary: Includes Rhine Riesling in the documented or permitted assortment of relevant Knjaževac and Negotin subregions and provides regional conditions, but does not rank it above all local white cultivars.
notes: A permitted or recorded assortment is not a comparative blind tasting and gives no «best white» title.

title: Frontiers in Plant Science 2024 — genetic characterization of old Serbian grapevines
provenance: Peer-reviewed original SSR/SNP and historical research
summary: Explicitly identifies Grašac as the local Vojvodina synonym for the white-berried cultivar Welschriesling and discusses its long Serbian history under that identity.
notes: The paper establishes identity; separate catalogue and encyclopedic evidence establishes Welschriesling's non-identity with Rhine Riesling.

title: Wines of Serbia — Grašac Beli: The Serbian White Grape Guide
provenance: Current Wines of Serbia editorial guide citing the 2024 genetic study
summary: States directly that Grašac Beli is Welschriesling/Italian Riesling, is not Rhine Riesling, and should not be mistaken for Rajnski rizling; it treats Grašac as a historically rooted and legitimate Serbian wine identity.
notes: «True Riesling» can disambiguate a label, but the distinct Grašac cultivar should not be framed as fake.

title: Vino.rs — Najbolja vina Srbije 2025: Dubravka Gold 2024
summary: Identifies Dubravka Gold 2024 as a Riesling/Sauvignon Blanc blend and a Best Buy; the abbreviated varietal wording does not distinguish Rhine from Italian Riesling, which the producer's exact declaration resolves as Italian Riesling.
notes: For exact composition, the producer's percentages and explicit cultivar names have priority over the article's shorthand «Riesling».

title: English Wikipedia — Riesling
summary: Defines Rhine-origin Riesling, includes Serbia among countries with significant plantings, and explicitly states that Welschriesling/Italian Riesling is an unrelated cultivar despite the shared name.
notes: It contains no three-region Serbian inventory, Negotin quality ranking or Dubravka product composition.

title: German Wikipedia — Riesling
summary: Identifies Riesling/Rheinriesling as a high-quality late-ripening cultivar and explicitly distinguishes the Rheinriesling name from popular Welschriesling usage.
notes: No Serbian regional distribution, comparative Negotin result or Dubravka blend is supplied.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Rajnai rizling
summary: Treats Rajnai rizling as the «real Rhine Riesling», lists Rhine/White Riesling synonyms and gives general origin, viticulture and wine-style information.
notes: It does not establish the three Serbian regions, a Negotin rank or a Džervin recipe.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Ризлинг
summary: Identifies Riesling as a Rhine-origin German white cultivar also known as Rajnski rizling and notes its popularity in Serbia; the linked Graševina article separately says Graševina/Italian Riesling is unrelated.
notes: It contains no Knjaževac–Negotin–Fruška inventory, quality comparison or Dubravka formula.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Рислинг and Вельшрислинг
summary: States explicitly that Welschriesling is unrelated to Riesling despite the similar name; the Riesling article supplies the separate international cultivar profile.
notes: Neither article provides the local Serbian regional ranking or Dubravka label evidence.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Graševina
summary: Lists Graševina's Welschriesling, Riesling Italico and related synonyms and describes it as its own white cultivar and wine tradition.
notes: The page is sparse and does not itself state the genetic nonrelationship, so stronger scientific and English/Russian references control that point.

title: UC Davis Foundation Plant Services — Pinot blanc
provenance: University grape variety registry using international catalogue nomenclature
summary: Lists Burgundac Beli among the documented synonyms of Pinot Blanc.
notes: The local Serbian word order Beli burgundac is independently used in Serbian wine references and English Wikipedia.

title: UC Davis Foundation Plant Services — Pinot gris
provenance: University grape variety registry using VIVC-linked synonym data
summary: Lists Burgundac Sivi and Sivi Pinot among the synonyms of Pinot Gris, alongside Pinot Grigio and other international names.
notes: The synonym record proves cultivar identity, not a particular Serbian vineyard share or style.

title: Zvonko Bogdan Winery — Pinot Blanc
provenance: Official winery product and vineyard specification
summary: Declares a 100% Pinot Blanc from Palić vineyards and gives four hectares for the wine, directly documenting a substantial named modern Palić block.
notes: The page intermittently returns a gateway error but remains publicly indexed; it does not identify the four hectares' complete soil profile.

title: Zvonko Bogdan Winery — 8 Guitar Players
provenance: Official winery wine and vineyard specification
summary: Lists Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Grigio and Pinot Blanc from Radić, Ludaš and Palić, with 15 hectares assigned to the wine, confirming both Pinot cultivars in a major modern northern Vojvodina portfolio.
notes: The combined locations and area do not allocate hectares or soils separately to each cultivar.

title: Park Palić — Petra Winery
provenance: Official Palić destination and wine-route profile
summary: Places Petra directly beside Lake Palić, records modern plantings beginning in 2009 including Pinot Grigio, and describes the vineyard soil as rich in clay and loam with a humus layer.
notes: The site lies within the broader Subotica wine landscape but is not described as pure sand, demonstrating why exact vineyard soil matters.

title: Wine Routes in Vojvodina Province, Northern Serbia
provenance: Peer-reviewed regional wine-tourism and geography study
summary: Describes the 24,000-hectare Subotica–Horgoš sandland and its vineyards but lists heterogeneous soils including sand, moving sand, clay, chernozem with sand and brown steppe soils.
notes: A regional geomorphological name cannot substitute for a parcel-level soil analysis.

title: New Europe Wine Guide — Serbia 2026
provenance: Beth Willard's current guide and its reproduction of the 2024 Serbian commercial Vineyard Register leaders
summary: The register-derived leading-white list contains Grašac 11%, Chardonnay 9%, Riesling 6% and Sauvignon Blanc 5%, not either white Pinot. The guide nevertheless documents modern Pinot Blanc and Pinot Grigio wines across Serbia, including Vojvodina examples, and scores Zvonko Bogdan Pinot Blanc 2022 at 95.
notes: A 268-wine guide is not a planting census; its register summary is used only to test the unqualified national «foundation» wording.

title: English Wikipedia — Pinot blanc and Pinot gris
summary: The Pinot Blanc article explicitly lists Beli burgundac as a Serbian name; the Pinot Gris article identifies Pinot Grigio as the same globally grown cultivar and emphasizes its broad regional and stylistic range.
notes: The articles contain no Vojvodina share, modern Serbian planting hierarchy or parcel-level Palić soil evidence.

title: German Wikipedia — Weißer Burgunder and Pinot gris
summary: Lists Burgundac Beli for Pinot Blanc and Burgundac Sivi for Pinot Gris in the two cultivar articles, and describes both as internationally distributed members of the Pinot family.
notes: No Serbian regional area statistics or Palić soil allocation is present.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Fehér burgundi and Szürkebarát
summary: Identifies Fehér burgundi as Pinot Blanc and Szürkebarát/Burgundi szürke as Pinot Gris/Pinot Grigio, providing neighbouring-language Pinot nomenclature and international context.
notes: It does not cover Vojvodina plantings, Palić or Serbian register ranks.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Пино гри and Виноградарство у Србији
summary: The Pinot Gris article says the cultivar is grown in Serbia under the name Burgundac sivi, while the national viticulture article lists both Burgundac beli and Burgundac sivi among Serbian cultivars.
notes: The corpus gives no current Vojvodina share or evidence that both varieties form the basis of modern Palić plantings.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Пино-блан and Пино-гри
summary: Treats Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris as distinct white-wine members of the Pinot mutation group and lists Burgundac sivi among Pinot Gris synonyms.
notes: Neither article quantifies Serbian plantings or identifies Palić vineyard soils.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Pinot bijeli and Pinot sivi
summary: Identifies Pinot bijeli/Pinot Blanc with Burgundac bijeli and maintains separate Pinot sivi material, giving adjacent South Slavic naming context.
notes: It contains no evidence about Vojvodina, the Serbian commercial register or Palić sands.

title: Plantgrape / INRAE–IFV — Semillon
provenance: French national technical catalogue of cultivated vine varieties
summary: Describes Sémillon as capable, under favourable conditions and managed yields, of full-bodied high-quality dry whites with moderate-to-low acidity, barrel ageing potential and liqueur wines.
notes: This is cultivar potential from professional tastings, not evidence that every Serbian bottle has low acidity or waxy texture.

title: Vino Župa — History of Župa
provenance: Long-established regional producer's history and current regional inventory
summary: Lists Sémillon among current Župa plantings and describes the post-WWII cooperative setting from which Vino Župa emerged.
notes: It does not date Župa's first Sémillon planting or trace a present parcel to a Yugoslav-era vineyard.

title: Vinarija Raj — Zenit
summary: Places the winery at Rajac in Negotinska Krajina and presents Zenit as a varietal Sémillon, calling the cultivar rare in Serbia and available at only a few other wineries; an archival 2017 vintage is also noted.
notes: The page does not publish acidity, full technical composition beyond the varietal wording, vineyard age or national label counts.

title: Vinarija Frunza Aglaja — vineyards and Sauvignon & Semillon
provenance: Official Negotin winery vineyard and wine declarations
summary: States that Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon grow in the Smedovac vineyard of the Rajac area and identifies Aglaja Sauvignon & Semillon as a structured, intensely fresh citrus wine with a mineral finish.
notes: No percentages, vintage, analytical acidity or separate Sémillon sensory profile are published on the landing page.

title: Vinarija Eden — estate vineyard and Sémillon 2018
provenance: Official Šumadija producer site and linked Sémillon technical card
summary: Dates the seven-hectare estate vineyard and its Sémillon to 2014–2015 and documents a sold-out 100% Sémillon 2018 naturally sweet wine, 10.5% alcohol and inox ageing, described through ripe fig, concentration, balance, full body and sweetness.
notes: An archived sweet half-bottle cannot establish the current national balance of varietal and blended Sémillon.

title: Časopis Vino — Suveren na vinskom tronu
provenance: Serbian specialist historical feature on the royal Oplenac vineyard
summary: Includes Sémillon among the French and German cultivars planted for the royal Oplenac wine programme in the late 1920s and records its use with Sauvignon Blanc in Oplenka.
notes: This is a secondary historical account rather than a parcel ledger, and it does not prove continuity into a current vineyard.

title: English Wikipedia — Sémillon
summary: Describes Sémillon as producing dry and sweet wines, generally heavy with low acidity and an oily texture, and documents both blended and varietal international styles.
notes: Serbia is not treated, so the article cannot establish Župa/Negotin history or national blend frequency.

title: German Wikipedia — Sémillon
summary: Describes powerful, long-lived dry and sweet wines and the common Bordeaux blend with Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle, while also recognising dry varietal use.
notes: It lists no Serbian regions, history, current products or production ratio.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — search: Sémillon
summary: No dedicated Hungarian Sémillon article was found; broader grape and regional pages only identify it as an international white variety.
notes: The corpus contributes no evidence for the Serbian locations, history, style or frequency claim.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Семијон
summary: Gives general French origin and honey, lemon and lime descriptors and names major foreign countries of cultivation, but does not mention Serbian vineyards despite being the local-language article.
notes: Its sweet-tasting generalisation does not fit all dry or blended Serbian wines and does not verify the book's regional assertions.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Семильон
summary: Provides general ampelography, international distribution and one Crimean varietal example, illustrating that Sémillon can be bottled varietally.
notes: It contains no Župa, Negotin, Yugoslav history or national blend-versus-varietal denominator.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — search: Semillon
summary: No dedicated Croatian Semillon article or Serbian regional material was found in the requested corpus.
notes: The absence supplies no positive or negative evidence about Serbian cultivation or wine style.

title: Plantgrape / INRAE–IFV — Cabernet-Sauvignon
provenance: French national technical catalogue of cultivated vine varieties
summary: States that properly mature Cabernet Sauvignon produces deep-coloured wines with an important tannic structure, ageing and wood-maturation capacity, while vegetal aromas recede as maturity advances.
notes: It does not provide Serbian regional distribution or support an invariant blackcurrant–cedar–tobacco profile.

title: CEVVIN — Kaberne sovinjon
provenance: Serbian Centre for Viticulture and Winemaking cultivar inventory
summary: Says Cabernet is grown throughout Serbia, ranks third by commercial vineyard area and has its largest regional areas in Tri Morave, Srem and Šumadija; it also describes young wines as coarse and the cultivar as sugar-accumulating and suitable for wood ageing.
notes: The page does not publish exact regional hectares or a snapshot year, but its explicit top-three hierarchy contradicts an area-based Negotin-first reading.

title: Ministry of Agriculture of Serbia — Wine Treasure of Serbia: Negotinska Krajina
provenance: Official Serbian protected-origin regional guide, English text edition
summary: Characterises Negotinska Krajina reds as extracted and higher-to-high in alcohol while fresh nights preserve moderate acids, aromatic complexity and colour, and describes the region's terrain, Danube/Timok influence and porous soils.
