provenance: Required Russian Wikipedia check with targeted Tamjanika search
summary: Supports that Muscats are a plural group with complicated historical assumptions, while the Russian Serbian-wine material calls Tamjanika a local white-Muscat mutation; it does not delimit the Serbian population or verify the current Alsace formula.
notes: The local-mutation wording is not an accession-level genetic result.

title: Croatian Wikipedia search — Tamjanika, Muškat sitnog zrna and Muškat ottonel
summary: No sufficiently specific Croatian Wikipedia evidence was found for the genetic scope of Serbian Tamjanika or the exact Alsace labelling and blending claim.
notes: Cognate cultivar names are insufficient to establish identity or sensory equivalence.

title: CEVVIN — Tamjanika bela
provenance: Serbia's Centre for Viticulture and Winemaking cultivar profile
summary: Groups Tamjanika, Tamjanika bela/žuta, Muscat à Petits Grains and Frontignan names together but explicitly records disagreement over whether the white and yellow forms are the same cultivar and therefore presents a variable group without prejudging origin.
notes: The profile's caution is compatible with a genetic result for a named accession but blocks extrapolation to every Serbian Tamjanika.

title: VIVC passport — MUSCAT A PETITS GRAINS BLANCS
provenance: Vitis International Variety Catalogue, variety number 8193
summary: Registers Muscat à Petits Grains Blancs as VIVC 8193 and lists Balkan Tamjanika/Tamnjanika Bela spellings among its synonyms.
notes: Catalogue synonymy is strong nomenclatural evidence but does not establish that every locally grouped vine sold under the broad name has been genotyped.

title: Tello et al. — The genetic characterization of grapevines prospected in old Serbian vineyards reveals multiple relationships between traditional varieties of the Balkans
summary: Genetically identifies five white-berried vines collected as Tamjanika Ćilibarka with Muscat à Petits Grains and proposes that local name as a synonym of Muscat à Petits Grains Blancs; it separately notes other Balkan Tamjanika family names.
notes: The sample result is decisive for Ćilibarka but does not claim exhaustive coverage of the entire commercial Tamjanika bela group.

title: Crespan and Milani — The Muscats: A molecular analysis of synonyms, homonyms and genetic relationships within a large family of grapevine cultivars
summary: Calls Muscats a large widespread family; analysis at two isozymes and 25 microsatellite loci reduced 64 accessions to 20 distinct molecular profiles and 44 synonyms, documenting extensive diversity, synonymy and homonymy.
notes: The family label is practical rather than a formal taxonomic rank, and shared Muscat flavour does not make all named types one cultivar.

title: CIVA — Muscat d’Alsace
summary: Says two Muscat types are grown in Alsace—Petits Grains and Ottonel—and that Muscat d’Alsace is most often their blend; describes the regional style as dry, fragrant, fresh and grape-like.
notes: The public-facing page groups colour forms under Petits Grains, whereas the legal text separately names white and rose Petits Grains.

title: Legifrance — consolidated ordinance defining Alsace controlled appellations
summary: Maps the Alsace varietal designation Muscat to Muscat à Petits Grains Blancs, Muscat à Petits Grains Roses and Muscat Ottonel.
notes: This is the controlling enumeration; the book names two of the three legal entries and omits the rose form.

title: Plantgrape — Muscat à Petits Grains Blancs
provenance: INRAE, Institut Agro Montpellier and IFV grape catalogue
summary: Provides the cultivar's distinct SSR profile, mid-season maturity about two weeks after Chasselas and potential for dry, sweet and sparkling wines with high sugar, balanced acidity and intense, powerful, delicate flavour.
notes: A cultivar profile establishes potential, not the inevitable sensory profile of every Alsace bottle.

title: Plantgrape — Muscat Ottonel
provenance: INRAE, Institut Agro Montpellier and IFV grape catalogue
summary: Provides a separate SSR profile and Chasselas × Muscat d’Eisenstadt origin, early maturity concurrent with Chasselas and potential for aromatic dry and liqueur wines.
notes: The profile confirms distinction from Petits Grains but not a universal tasting outcome across sites and winemaking regimes.

title: English Wikipedia — Welschriesling
summary: Lists Riesling Italico, Italian Riesling, Graševina and Grašac among the names of Welschriesling, assigns VIVC 13217, places the cultivar in Austria, Croatia and Serbia, and explicitly distinguishes it from Rhine Riesling.
notes: The identity fields trace substantially to VIVC and the country summaries share secondary reference traditions, so this is not counted as an independent genetic study.

title: German Wikipedia — Welschriesling
summary: Maps Welschriesling to Riesling Italico, Italian Riesling and Graševina under VIVC 13217, states that it is not related to Rhine/White Riesling, and gives Coccalona Nera × unknown as its current pedigree.
notes: The article follows Austrian institutional and genetic sources; its categorical wording is interpreted as absence of close documented relationship, not proof against every remote ancestor.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Olaszrizling
summary: Treats Olaszrizling, Welschriesling, Taljanska grasevina, Riesling Italien and Italian Riesling as names of one cultivar and records its cultivation in Austria and Croatia.
notes: The page does not name Grašac or directly discuss Rhine Riesling, so it supports the synonym and geographic parts but not the literal nonrelation claim.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Грашевина
summary: Identifies Graševina with Riesling Italico and Italian Riesling, distinguishes it from Rhine Riesling, and lists Austria, Croatia and Serbia among cultivation countries.
notes: The short page does not expose primary genetic evidence or the specifically Vojvodinian form Grašac, which is supplied by Tello et al. and current Serbian guidance.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Вельшрислинг
summary: Gives VIVC 13217, names Riesling Italico, Italian Riesling and Graševina as synonyms, describes Austrian and Croatian use, and explicitly says that the cultivar is not Rhine Riesling.
notes: Its identity and relationship wording is derivative of VIVC and shared international references rather than a separate genetic result.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Graševina
summary: Uses Graševina as the Croatian cultivar name and lists Riesling Italico, Welschriesling and Olasz Rizling among other names.
notes: The legacy page does not explicitly compare Rhine Riesling and acknowledges weak source history, so official Vinacroatia and primary catalogue evidence carry more weight.

title: VIVC passport 13217 — WELSCHRIESLING
provenance: Vitis International Variety Catalogue, Julius Kühn-Institut
summary: Registers Welschriesling as the white wine-grape cultivar VIVC 13217; indexed catalogue records and linked nomenclature anchor its international synonym set separately from Riesling Weiss.
notes: Direct automated opening was blocked, so the entry is used only for its indexed identity fields and the separately corroborated synonym tradition, not for an unobserved relationship claim.

title: VIVC passport 10077 — RIESLING WEISS
provenance: Vitis International Variety Catalogue, Julius Kühn-Institut
summary: Registers Riesling Weiss as the distinct white wine-grape cultivar VIVC 10077, of German origin, rather than as an entry or synonym under Welschriesling VIVC 13217.
notes: Separate catalogue numbers establish distinct cultivar identities; by themselves they do not prove the absence of every remote common ancestor.

title: Raimondi et al. — DNA-based genealogy reconstruction of Nebbiolo, Barbera and other ancient grapevine cultivars from northwestern Italy
provenance: Scientific Reports 10 (2020), peer-reviewed grapevine genealogy study
summary: Identifies Coccalona Nera as one parent of Riesling Italico/Welschriesling/Graševina while leaving the other parent unknown; the current pedigree therefore supports a distinct identity but is incomplete.
notes: The open article presented a reCAPTCHA during this access; its result is also reproduced in later peer-reviewed parentage literature and was previously captured in the audit. It does not test or exclude every remote relationship to Rhine Riesling.

title: Austrian Wine — Welschriesling
provenance: Austrian Wine Marketing Board official cultivar profile
summary: Uses Welschriesling as the Austrian cultivar name, identifies Riesling Italico as its northern-Italian name and names Elbling as its closest relative.
notes: The page was visible in indexed text but direct opening returned an internal retrieval error; it supports Austrian nomenclature and the absence of Rhine Riesling as the named nearest relative, not an absolute universal nonrelation theorem.

title: Vinacroatia — Graševina cultivar profile
provenance: Croatian Chamber of Economy / Wines of Croatia official cultivar material
summary: Uses Graševina as the Croatian name and lists Welschriesling, Laški rizling, Olasz rizling, Vlašsky ryzlink and Riesling Italico as its most frequent synonyms.
notes: This establishes cultivar nomenclature, not identical wine style across countries.

title: Vinacroatia — Croatian wine regions
provenance: Croatian Chamber of Economy / Wines of Croatia official regional overview
summary: Explicitly presents Graševina (Welschriesling) as Croatia's most widely grown variety and describes its broad range of Croatian wine styles.
notes: The parenthetical equivalence is decisive for the country-name claim; the style range also cautions against reading cultivar identity as sensory uniformity.

title: SerbianWine.rs — Grašac Beli: The Serbian White Grape Guide
provenance: Current Serbian public wine guide dated 4 August 2026, with linked genetic source
summary: Calls Grašac Beli the historic Serbian and especially Vojvodinian name for Welschriesling, lists Graševina, Riesling Italico and Italian Riesling as names of the same cultivar, and warns that Rhine Riesling is a different grape.
notes: This is recent secondary guidance; Tello et al. supplies the peer-reviewed basis for the Grašac/Welschriesling local-synonym statement.

title: Tello et al. — The genetic characterization of grapevines prospected in old Serbian vineyards reveals multiple relationships between traditional varieties of the Balkans
summary: States that Grašac is the local name used in Vojvodina for the white-berried Welschriesling cultivar and documents Beli Grašac in a Fruška Gora source from 1816.
notes: The passage establishes current nomenclature and historical use; it does not make Grašac the preferred legal name in Austria or Croatia.

title: Wikipedia — Grüner Veltliner
summary: Describes a very wide style range: simple Weinviertel examples may have fresh acidity and crisp fruit, while fuller wines show pepper, mineral and citrus notes; it also says young Grüner is usually not very aromatic and that white pepper can be absent even in classic examples.
notes: The article contains no Kreaca comparison and cannot establish a closest sensory match.

title: Wikipedia — Grüner Veltliner
summary: Characterizes good Grüner Veltliner as fresh and potentially intense in bouquet, with white pepper, tobacco, citrus and peach among the cited notes.
notes: No direct Kreaca comparison or controlled acidity ranking is present.

title: Wikipédia — Zöld veltelini
summary: Presents the wine as lively in acidity, fresh, usually light, fruity and spicy, with pepper and fruit descriptors, and mentions high-acid material for sparkling wine.
notes: The page itself carries sourcing-quality warnings and contains no Kreaca comparison, so it is contextual rather than decisive evidence.

title: Википедија — претрага Креаца и Гринер велтлинер
summary: No relevant Serbian Wikipedia cultivar article or passage comparing Kreaca with Grüner Veltliner was found.
notes: An absence result documents corpus coverage only; it is not evidence that the sensory resemblance is false.

title: Википедия — Грюнер Вельтлинер
summary: Notes the cultivar's broad range of wine styles and recurrent fruit, spice and freshly ground pepper descriptors.
notes: It does not mention Kreaca or provide a comparative acidity ranking.

title: Wikipedija — Dodatak: Popis vinskih sorti
summary: Lists Kreaca bijela or Kreacer and Veltlinac zeleni as separate grape entries but gives no sensory comparison between them.
notes: The list supports corpus coverage and distinct entries only, not similarity or dissimilarity in wine style.

title: CEVVIN — Kreaca
provenance: Serbian Centre for Viticulture and Oenology cultivar profile
summary: Describes the berry taste as neutral and the wine as harmonious and drinkable, in a better-quality mass-wine group; it does not call Kreaca sharply acidic or compare it with Grüner Veltliner.
notes: Neutral berry taste is not equivalent to aroma-free wine, and harmonious or drinkable does not quantify acidity.

title: Vinogradar, vinogradar-rasadničar, podrumar — Kreaca profile
provenance: Yugoslav technical viticulture and cellar manual, 1964
summary: Places Kreaca in the third ripening epoch, gives a historical typical wine range of 10–12% alcohol and 5–6 per mille acidity, and calls the wine drinkable, harmonious and characteristically varietal in aroma.
notes: These dated typical figures are neither current legal limits nor a controlled comparison with Grüner Veltliner.

title: RTV — Sinonim za grožđe Kreaca je Banatski rizling
provenance: Radio Television of Vojvodina local report
summary: Describes Kreaca wines as white, harmonious and drinkable without a strong aroma; a local producer compares their quality with Hungarian Ezerjó rather than Grüner Veltliner.
notes: Producer testimony is useful local evidence but is not a blind comparative tasting or cultivar-wide measurement.

title: Austrian Wine — Grüner Veltliner
provenance: Austrian Wine Marketing Board official cultivar profile
summary: States that Grüner Veltliner spans all quality levels, from light more acidic wines to highly ripe Prädikatswein, demonstrating that acidity and body are not a single fixed cultivar style.
notes: The indexed official text was available while direct opening returned a retrieval error; it contains no Kreaca comparison.

title: Austrian Wine — Weinviertel
provenance: Austrian Wine Marketing Board official regional profile
summary: Describes Weinviertel Grüner Veltliner through pepper notes, a fruity bouquet and fresh acidity, supporting one recognizable regional style rather than a universal cultivar-wide intensity ranking.
notes: Regional typicity cannot establish that Grüner is the closest analogue for Kreaca.

title: Wikipedia — Kadarka and Zweigelt
provenance: English Wikipedia cultivar articles and internal search
summary: Treats Kadarka as an old Central European and Balkan cultivar with competing Hungarian and Shkodër-region origin hypotheses; the separate Zweigelt article identifies an Austrian 1922 St. Laurent × Blaufränkisch crossing but supplies almost no general sensory comparison.
notes: The Kadarka sensory paragraph is weakly sourced and conflicts with stronger national profiles; no Kadarka–Zweigelt equivalence is stated.

title: Wikipedia — Kadarka und Zweigelt
summary: Identifies Zweigelt as an Austrian St. Laurent × Blaufränkisch crossing and describes substantial fruity violet-red wines with sour-cherry aroma and soft tannins, while the Kadarka article allows slight spice but also dark, tannic, extract-rich ageworthy wines.
notes: The two profiles demonstrate possible overlap and large internal variation, not a measured nearest match.

title: Wikipédia — Kadarka és Zweigelt
summary: Presents Kadarka's exact origin as uncertain between Balkan or Asia-Minor traditions and the separate Zweigelt page as an Austrian 1922 Kékfrankos × Szent Lőrinc crossing; no direct sensory ranking of the pair is supplied.
notes: The Zweigelt sensory material is sparse and poorly sourced; official national wine pages carry greater weight.

title: Википедија — Кадарка и претрага Цвајгелта
provenance: Serbian Wikipedia cultivar article and targeted Zweigelt search
summary: Describes Kadarka as elegant, light, harmonious and cherry-led with moderate acidity; no dedicated Serbian Zweigelt cultivar article or direct pair comparison was found, only broader mentions of the Austrian variety.
notes: Useful local-language style context, but not an independent controlled tasting.

title: Википедия — Кадарка и Цвайгельт
provenance: Russian Wikipedia Kadarka article and Friedrich Zweigelt article
summary: The brief Kadarka article supplies names and regional cultivation but little sensory evidence; the Friedrich Zweigelt article confirms the 1922 St. Laurent × Blaufränkisch crossing and Austrian identity of the variety.
notes: No Russian Wikipedia sensory comparison of the two cultivars was found.

title: Wikipedija — Kadarka i Zweigelt
summary: Describes Kadarka as ruby, medium-bodied, soft and fresh and Zweigelt as ruby-coloured with herb, bay-leaf and red- or black-currant aromas, usually drunk young; it also confirms Zweigelt's Blaufränkisch × St. Laurent origin.
notes: The overlap is descriptive and may reflect shared secondary sources; it does not establish closest similarity.

title: CEVVIN — Skadarka
provenance: Serbian Centre for Viticulture and Oenology cultivar profile
summary: Uses Skadarka with Kadarka among its synonyms, calls it Balkan and probably connected with the Lake Skadar area, and describes aromatic wine from both sandy and bound soils, while acknowledging strong vintage and crop effects.
notes: The precise Lake Skadar birthplace is a hypothesis disputed by other specialist sources; CEVVIN does not compare the wine with Zweigelt.

title: Magyar Bor — Kadarka
summary: Calls Kadarka most likely Balkan while stating that its exact origin is unknown; describes medium ruby-purple colour, red berries and cherry, fresh spices, herbs and florals, light-to-medium body, restrained tannins and bright acidity, and says it is often compared with Pinot Noir.
notes: The named established comparison is Pinot Noir rather than Zweigelt; the page also recognizes Kadarka as a Carpathian Basin local variety by cultural adoption.

title: Magyar Bor — Red wine
provenance: Official Hungarian Wine overview of red-wine styles
summary: Places Kékfrankos, Kadarka, Zweigelt and Portugieser together among varieties that can produce fruity light wines in the climatic conditions of the Carpathian Basin.
notes: Grouping the varieties by a broad regional style does not rank them as closest analogues or guarantee the same body and aroma in every bottle.

title: Austrian Wine — Zweigelt
provenance: Austrian Wine Marketing Board official cultivar profile
summary: Identifies Zweigelt as Austria's most widespread red cultivar and the St. Laurent × Blaufränkisch crossing created in Klosterneuburg in 1922; fully ripe grapes can yield full-bodied, morello-cherry wines with good longevity.
notes: The indexed official text was available while direct opening returned 403; it contains no Kadarka comparison.

title: Austrian Wine — Come to the fresh side: Austria's juicy red wines
provenance: Austrian Wine Marketing Board official style overview
summary: Describes an easy-drinking Zweigelt style with cherry and berry fruit, rounded velvety tannins and moderate alcohol, demonstrating the lighter pole that can overlap with modern Kadarka.
notes: This is a style category, not a cultivar-wide limit or direct comparison with Kadarka.

title: Austrian Wine — Neusiedlersee
provenance: Austrian Wine Marketing Board official regional profile
summary: Calls dry Neusiedlersee DAC Zweigelt fruity, spicy and harmonious with heart-cherry aroma and places the region in the hot, dry continental Pannonian climate zone.
notes: Regional DAC typicity is narrower than all Zweigelt and is Pannonian rather than a generic Alpine category.

title: Austrian Wine — The Pannonian Region
provenance: Austrian Wine Marketing Board official climate-zone profile
summary: Presents the eastern Pannonian area as Austria's principal red-wine zone and specifically identifies full-bodied Zweigelt as dominant between Carnuntum and the Seewinkel.
notes: Austria contains Alpine landscapes, but its leading Zweigelt territory is officially framed as continental Pannonian wine country.

title: VIVC — Zweigeltrebe Blau pedigree confirmed by markers
summary: Records marker-confirmed parentage of Zweigeltrebe Blau as Saint Laurent and Blaufränkisch.
notes: Parentage establishes cultivar origin but does not predict sensory similarity to Kadarka.

title: Plantgrape — Kadarka
provenance: INRAE, IFV and Institut Agro Montpellier national grape-variety database
summary: Places Kadarka historically in Hungary and the Balkans with possible Ottoman origin and describes aromatic, not deeply coloured wines with good tannic structure and alcohol under favourable conditions and managed yields.
notes: The profile shows that pale colour can coexist with structure and does not make medium body or a Zweigelt analogy universal.

title: Wikipedia — Garganega and Bagrina search
provenance: English Wikipedia Garganega article and targeted Bagrina search
summary: Describes controlled-yield Soave Classico Garganega through delicate lemon, almond and spice and notes substantial yield-dependent variation; no standalone English Bagrina article or direct Bagrina–Garganega comparison was found.
notes: The article supports neither the apricot/quince-versus-citrus dichotomy nor a nearest-analogue ranking.

title: Wikipedia — Garganega und Bagrina-Suche
provenance: German Wikipedia Garganega article and targeted Bagrina search
summary: Gives Garganega light almond and lemon aromas and a yield-dependent range from thin neutral wine to dense full wine; no dedicated German Bagrina profile or pair comparison was found.
notes: It demonstrates Garganega's internal range but does not establish creaminess, quince or a measured similarity to Bagrina.

title: Wikipédia-keresés — Bagrina és Garganega
summary: No dedicated Hungarian profiles or direct comparison covering Bagrina and Garganega sensory descriptors, texture or finish were found.
notes: The Hungarian-language corpus cannot verify any element of the proposed anchor.

title: Википедија — Багрина и Гарганега
provenance: Serbian Wikipedia Bagrina and Garganega cultivar articles
summary: The Bagrina page gives Serbian and Negotin identity and only an unspecific distinctive taste; the separate Garganega page lists lemon, almond and spice for controlled-yield Soave and thin neutral wines at excessive yields. Neither article compares the pair.
notes: Both standalone pages now exist, but they provide no apricot, quince, creaminess or mineral-tension evidence for Bagrina and appear unsuitable for a nearest-analogue claim.

title: Википедия — Гарганега и поиск Багрины
provenance: Russian Wikipedia Garganega article and targeted Bagrina search
summary: Covers Garganega identity, history, cultivation and the risk of neutral watery wine at uncontrolled yields; no Russian Bagrina article or sensory comparison of the pair was found.
notes: The page provides no support for the proposed fruit, texture or finish equivalence.

title: Wikipedija — popis sorti Bagrina i Garganega
provenance: Croatian Wikipedia wine-grape list and targeted searches
summary: The Croatian list names both Bagrina and Garganega but supplies no cultivar profiles, descriptors or relationship; no dedicated comparative article was found.
notes: A name list cannot support sensory equivalence or any individual descriptor.

title: Darko Jakšić, ed. — Sorta vinove loze Bagrina
provenance: CEVVIN, Niš, 2023, 164 pp., ISBN 978-86-912489-3-2; sensory section pp. 130–147
summary: The 21 Bagrina microvinifications show a broad fruit, floral and herbal spectrum with sample-dependent acidity, bitterness and structure; apple, peach, flowers and occasional honey, mint and spice occur, while no single compact apricot–quince–cream–mineral profile characterises the entire set.
notes: The monograph does not compare Bagrina with Garganega; selected Matalj bottle descriptors must not be projected onto all experimental material.

title: Vino.rs — Bagrina kakvu nismo poznavali
provenance: On-site report from the 2023 Bagrina project conclusion and tasting
summary: Reports the 13,110-vine survey, 21 selected genotypes and a wide sensory range; fruit, floral, citrus and some herbal impressions occurred, directly showing that citrus is possible in Bagrina rather than excluded by apricot or quince.
notes: The report contains no Garganega comparison and cannot make any one fruit descriptor universal.

title: JUG deli — Matalj Bagrina Bukovska 2021
provenance: Retail card reproducing a detailed Matalj tasting note
summary: For the 2021 wine, lists apricot, fresh quince, hay, wildflowers and herbs, with moderately full body, juiciness and a mineral or tense palate impression.
notes: Producer-derived and vintage-specific; it neither proves a generic Bagrina profile nor compares the wine with Garganega.

title: Vinoteka Beograd — Matalj Bagrina Bukovska vintage archive
provenance: Dated retail technical archive reproducing producer data
summary: Selected Matalj vintages include apricot and changing fruit, herb and floral notes together with full body, creamy texture, firmness and minerality; vessel and ageing information also changes by vintage.
notes: The archive demonstrates occurrence and vintage variation, not a cross-producer cultivar constant or direct Garganega equivalence.

title: Consorzio Tutela Vini Soave — The Grapes
provenance: Official Soave appellation consortium Garganega profile
summary: States that Garganega expression changes considerably with soils and winemaking: basalt can be steely and mineral, limestone can show white flower, apricot, sweet apple and citrus, and a slightly bitter-almond finish is common; the broader aroma map is diverse.
notes: Apricot and citrus explicitly coexist, disproving the proposed binary; the page does not mention Bagrina or identify it as an analogue.

title: Consorzio Tutela Vini Soave — The different faces of Soave wine
summary: Explains that Garganega can give a deep creamy texture especially in warm vintages and volcanic terroirs, with skin contact, lees ageing or light barrique among techniques used to develop textural richness; other Soave remains finer, lemony and fresh.
notes: The conditional and technique-dependent wording prevents creaminess from serving as an invariant varietal bridge to Bagrina.

title: Tai and Kostaki — The science of minerality
summary: Reviews the broad and experience-dependent mineral lexicon, the limited scientific understanding of its mechanisms and evidence that perceived minerality often lacks a clear relationship to mineral concentrations in wine or a simple soil-to-wine mineral profile.
notes: The review does not evaluate Bagrina or Garganega; it supports treating «mineral tension» as an operational sensory description rather than literal geological transfer.

title: Wikipedia — Dimiat and Cortese di Gavi
provenance: English Wikipedia Dimiat and Cortese di Gavi articles
summary: Identifies Smederevka as a Dimiat synonym and describes Dimiat wines as usually light-bodied and very aromatic; the separate Gavi article says the protected wine is made exclusively from Cortese. It supplies no direct sensory comparison, Serbian-author attribution or price explanation.
notes: The very-aromatic wording conflicts with a universal quiet-aroma template; Wikipedia does not establish market causality.

title: Wikipedia — Dimiat und Cortese di Gavi
provenance: German Wikipedia Dimiat and Cortese di Gavi articles
summary: Calls Dimiat wines simple and lightly fragrant; for Gavi it records protected origin, 100% Cortese, characteristic delicate scent, dry pleasant fresh harmonious taste and a 5.0 g/L minimum total acidity for still wine.
notes: The articles do not compare the cultivars or prove a price premium; the Gavi details derive from the official production rules.

title: Wikipédia-keresés — Smederevka, Cortese és Gavi
provenance: Hungarian Wikipedia targeted cultivar and wine search
summary: No dedicated Hungarian profiles or direct material covering the Smederevka–Cortese/Gavi comparison, sensory equivalence, Serbian author usage, pricing or reputation causality were found.
notes: The negative result documents corpus coverage only and is not counter-evidence.

title: Википедија — Смедеревка и претрага Кортезе/Gavi
provenance: Serbian Wikipedia Smederevka article and targeted Cortese/Gavi search
summary: The Smederevka page lists stone fruit, a slightly sour table-wine taste and spritzer use; no dedicated Cortese/Gavi article or direct comparison, author tradition, price claim or causal evidence was found in Serbian Wikipedia.
notes: The page contains old and disputed origin or production language and is weaker than current technical and specialist sources.

title: Википедия — Димят/Смедеревка и Гави
provenance: Russian Wikipedia Dimiat and Gavi articles
summary: Treats Smederevka as the same cultivar as Dimiat and gives a wide Dimiat style range; the Gavi article identifies Cortese and describes light, sufficiently acidic, very dry wine with apple, mineral, almond and citrus impressions. It does not compare the pair or establish price causality.
notes: The two articles support neither neutral taste nor an exact equality of acidity.

title: Wikipedija — popis sorti Cortese i Smederevka
provenance: Croatian Wikipedia wine-grape list and targeted searches
summary: The Croatian list names Cortese and Smederevka separately but supplies no profiles, relationship, author attribution, price comparison or regional-reputation analysis.
notes: A name list cannot validate any sensory or economic element of the proposed anchor.

title: CEVVIN — Smederevka
provenance: Serbian Centre for Viticulture and Oenology cultivar profile
summary: Reports must acidity sometimes around 9 g/L under high yields and describes finished wine as drinkable, light and pleasantly aromatic, sometimes vanilla-like; it also records blending use to raise acidity.
notes: Must chemistry cannot be directly equated with finished Gavi, and the profile makes the wine pleasantly aromatic rather than uniformly neutral.

title: NIN — Smederevka: Indigenous, timeless, and uniquely its own
summary: Describes Smederevka wines as light, fresh, drinkable and crisp, with lemon-led citrus, herbs, white flowers and possible vanillin and spice, and attributes blending and sparkling suitability to good acidity.
notes: The explicit aromatic descriptors undermine a blanket neutral-taste claim; the article does not compare Smederevka with Cortese.

title: Falstaff — Smederevka
summary: Identifies Smederevka with Dimyat, says fresh acidity supports sparkling wine and calls the wines overall rather neutral, while also documenting dry-to-sweet styles and current still and sparkling examples.
notes: Its neutral assessment conflicts with English Wikipedia and current Serbian aromatic descriptions, demonstrating that the descriptor is not universal.

title: Ivanova-Petropulos, Ilievski and Ailer — Influence of variety and vintage on the basic physico-chemical composition of Smederevka and Vranec wines
provenance: Journal of Agriculture and Plant Sciences 22(2), 2024, pp. 87–94, doi:10.46763/JAPS2422287ip
summary: For six Smederevka vintages from 2018–2023, reports total acidity of 4.8–7.2 g/L, average 5.74 g/L, with alcohol 10.21–11.0% and vintage variation; the authors call the acidity relatively high and adequate for freshness and stability.
notes: North Macedonian wines from one subregion and protocol do not establish all Serbian Smederevka or equality with Gavi.

title: Vino&Fino — Šansa za Smederevku
summary: Explicitly asks whether Smederevka can become a Serbian counterpart to Piedmontese Cortese, presents shared high acidity and an aroma range, and asserts that Cortese/Gavi has a much stronger reputation and higher price. It also describes Smederevka as fresh, crisp, citrus-, herb- and white-fruit-led rather than simply neutral.
notes: This is the traceable authorial source behind much of the book wording; its causal market explanation is an expert interpretation without a disclosed price sample or model.

title: WineJour — Wine Identity: Smederevka Masterclass
provenance: Serbian report of a 2016 Smederevka masterclass and vertical tasting
summary: Records «Toma» presenting Cortese/Gavi through high acidity, neutral taste, delicate aromas, regional reputation and high price as a reveal after the audience accepts the description for Smederevka; it also documents broad Smederevka styles and actual tasting variation.
notes: This is a report of Tomislav Ivanović's presentation, not an independent origin of the analogy; the quoted Cortese profile is not accompanied by a traceable underlying citation.

title: Consorzio Tutela del Gavi — The Gavi DOCG
provenance: Official Gavi appellation consortium denomination and sensory profile
summary: Describes the Gavi DOCG styles through elegant delicate scent with fresh fruit, white flowers, citrus and bitter almond, and a dry, full, pleasantly fresh, harmonious taste; it documents the protected 11-municipality territory and long regional identity.
notes: The profile contradicts neutral taste while supporting delicate aroma; official promotion of territory cannot quantify reputation's causal contribution to price.

title: Disciplinare di Produzione dei Vini DOCG Gavi o Cortese di Gavi
provenance: Italian Ministry of Agricultural, Food and Forestry Policies decree of 6 August 2021, published by Consorzio Tutela del Gavi
summary: Reserves every Gavi/Cortese di Gavi type to vineyards composed solely of Cortese; requires characteristic delicate scent, dry pleasant fresh harmonious taste and minimum total acidity of 5.0 g/L for basic types and 5.5 g/L for Riserva types.
notes: Legal minima define eligibility rather than actual market averages and do not measure similarity to Smederevka or willingness to pay.

title: Vinoteka Beograd — Cortese listings
provenance: Serbian specialist retailer, 12 Cortese/Gavi listings observed at access
summary: Lists 0.75 L Gavi wines from roughly 1,880 to 7,500 RSD, with most listings above 2,000 RSD and multiple producers and vintages represented.
notes: A retailer category is time-sensitive, may include unavailable stock and is not a representative market census; it cannot isolate reputation from import and producer effects.

title: Vinoteka Beograd — Vinarija Janko listings
provenance: Same Serbian specialist retailer used for the Gavi comparison
summary: Lists Janko Smederevka 2024, 0.75 L, at 1,160 RSD, providing a same-retailer basic domestic Smederevka comparator.
notes: One producer and vintage cannot define the full Smederevka market or willingness to pay.

title: Vinoteka Beograd — Matijašević Vinogradi listings
provenance: Same Serbian specialist retailer used for the Gavi comparison
summary: Lists 100% Smederevka Matijašević Belina 2022 at 1,480 RSD and skin-contact Belina Orange 2020 at 2,045 RSD, showing a domestic style range and overlap with entry Gavi.
notes: Different winemaking and vintages make the orange wine a useful counterexample to categorical non-premium status but not a like-for-like Gavi comparator.

title: Wine Art Shop — Michele Chiarlo Gavi Palás
provenance: Independent Serbian specialist retailer product page
summary: Lists a 0.75 L Gavi DOCG at 1,518 RSD regular and 1,138.50 RSD promotional price, with Cortese, producer and style specified; the sale price falls within or below observed Smederevka points.
notes: A temporary promotion cannot represent normal Gavi pricing, but it demonstrates that current consumer prices overlap and depend on retail conditions.

title: Wikipedia — Vranac, Negroamaro and Mourvèdre
provenance: English Wikipedia current articles for all three cultivars
summary: The newly expanded Vranac article, citing CANU and peer-reviewed work, gives full body, intense ruby colour, blackberry, blueberry, multiple styles and process-dependent phenolics. Separate articles call Negroamaro deeply coloured and rustic with earthy bitterness, and Mourvèdre potentially deeply coloured, very tannic and blackberry-led.
notes: The three articles do not compare the cultivars or establish a closest analogue; their sensory passages have unequal sourcing and must not be treated as one controlled dataset.

title: Wikipedia — Vranac, Negroamaro und Monastrell
summary: Vranac is linked only to deep wine colour; Negroamaro is described as producing powerful reds with blackcurrant and cherry; Monastrell/Mourvèdre is called dark, tannin-rich and in need of long bottle maturation to reduce astringency. No article makes the proposed three-way comparison.
notes: The categorical Monastrell ageing line is a generic secondary statement and cannot prove either a young-wine equivalence or Vranac's exact bottle-age requirement.

title: Wikipédia — Mourvèdre and targeted Vranac/Negroamaro search
provenance: Hungarian Wikipedia Mourvèdre article and targeted cultivar searches
summary: Identifies Mourvèdre as Spanish Monastrell and documents its principal regions, but supplies no useful sensory profile for the anchor. No dedicated Vranac or Negroamaro cultivar article with comparative tannin, fruit, body or ageing evidence was found.
notes: Name mentions in broader regional pages do not validate sensory similarity or ranking.

title: Википедија — Вранац и претрага Negroamaro/Monastrell
provenance: Serbian Wikipedia expanded Vranac article and targeted comparison-grape searches
summary: Citing CANU and research, it describes Vranac as full-bodied and intensely ruby with blackberry, blueberry and dried spice, explicitly notes multiple wine styles and explains that phenolics and winemaking affect astringency and ageing. No Serbian Wikipedia comparison with Negroamaro or Monastrell was found.
notes: The English and Serbian Vranac pages share much of the same source base and are not independent confirmations.

title: Википедия — Вранац, Мурведр/Монастрель и поиск Негроамаро
provenance: Russian Wikipedia Vranac and Mourvèdre articles plus targeted Negroamaro search
summary: The Vranac page states that after one or two years the wine is dark ruby and complex but does not discuss tannin and cites only an old tourism page for the wine section. The Mourvèdre page explicitly says taste depends on growing region; Negroamaro appears only in general lists, with no comparative profile.
notes: The exact timing is too weakly sourced to establish necessity; absence of a Negroamaro profile leaves the ranking unsupported.

title: Wikipedija — Vranac (vino) and targeted Negroamaro/Monastrell search
provenance: Croatian Wikipedia unsourced Vranac article and targeted comparison-grape searches
summary: Repeats the legacy formula of young purple jammy wine, strong tannins, a one-to-two-year transition and bottle or oak ageing often being necessary. It gives no references and no profiles of Negroamaro or Monastrell with which to test the proposed ranking.
notes: The text belongs to the same translation/reuse family as older English descriptions; lexical agreement with the book is not independent corroboration.

title: Montenegrin Academy of Sciences and Arts — Leksikon vinogradarstva i vinarstva Crne Gore: Vranac
provenance: Authoritative national-academy cultivar entry by Vesna Maraš
summary: Gives Vranac full body, intense ruby colour, blackberry, blueberry and dried spice, about 12–14% alcohol and 5–6 g/L wine acidity, and explicitly recognizes multiple wine profiles, styles and blending uses.
notes: It does not compare Vranac with Negroamaro or Monastrell, require a two-year bottle threshold or define every Vranac tannin as hard.

title: BKWine/Forbes — Vranec/Vranac grape profile
provenance: Independent specialist journalist profile by Per Karlsson
summary: Reports near-opaque dark colour, blackberry, blueberry, plum, cherry or cassis, spice, herbs and chocolate; says tannin and acidity are usually prominent but explicitly notes that tannins may be soft.
notes: A broad tasting synthesis, not a direct comparison with the two proposed Mediterranean anchors.

title: Raičević et al. — Polyphenolic content and sensory profile of Montenegrin Vranac
provenance: Peer-reviewed Macedonian Journal of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, DOI 10.20450/mjcce.2017.1145
summary: Experimentally shows that vintage, maceration system, enzyme, oak chips and added grape tannin change Vranac phenolics, colour and sensory profile.
notes: The study supports variability and possible maturation effects, not a mandatory two-year wait or a binary hard-versus-soft taxonomy.

title: WSET — Discovering Vranec and North Macedonia
provenance: Wine & Spirit Education Trust article created with a WSET School London expert webinar
summary: Describes varietal Vranec through opulent black fruit, blackberry, overripe Marasca cherry and prune, full body and velvety well-rounded tannins; its firm structure supports prolonged barrel and bottle ageing.
notes: Ageing capability is not a claim that young wine is inaccessible, and the article does not rank Monastrell against Negroamaro.

title: Decanter — World Vranec Day: DWWA 2025 wines
provenance: Current Decanter World Wine Awards synthesis and judged wine notes
summary: Calls Vranec deep red, full-bodied, high-tannin and ageworthy, then shows real texture variation across awarded wines: supple grainy, firm, firm grainy and robust tannins, with blackcurrant, bilberry, blackberry and plum recurring.
notes: Competition examples substantiate typical structure and variability but are not age-matched against Negroamaro or Monastrell.

title: Plantgrape — Mourvèdre
provenance: French national cultivar database maintained by INRAE, IFV and Institut Agro Montpellier
summary: Recognizes Monastrell as the Spanish official name and describes sufficiently ripe, low-yield Mourvèdre as aromatic, tannic, structured and suitable for ageing or wood, while calling its colour potential moderate and noting possible low acidity.
notes: The maturity and yield conditions and moderate colour warning prevent a universal young-Monastrell template.

title: DOP Jumilla — Our Grape Varieties: Monastrell
provenance: Official Jumilla protected designation council cultivar profile
summary: Describes Monastrell through powerful tannins, aromatic intensity, medium acidity, warmth and complexity, but also a silky mouth-feel; it notes thick skins, phenolic ripening and berry-ripeness variation.
notes: A regional Monastrell profile cannot represent every Mourvèdre worldwide and itself shows that power does not exclude softness.

title: DOP Jumilla — Wine Profiles
provenance: Official Jumilla protected designation council style profile
summary: Young reds are described as deeply purple-red, expressive in black fruits, plums, cherries and other fruit, with structure, power and lively but ripe tannins; unoaked or lightly oaked examples can also be fruity and refreshing, and newer styles are deliberately fresher and fruit-driven.
notes: The page covers Jumilla reds dominated by Monastrell rather than a controlled set of 100% varietal wines, so it supports a regional analogy, not equality.

title: MASAF — consolidated Salice Salentino DOC production rules
provenance: Italian Ministry of Agriculture decree of 19 May 2026 and consolidated disciplinare effective 28 May 2026
summary: Requires Salice Salentino labelled Negroamaro to contain at least 90% of the cultivar and describes the red as ruby, characteristically intense with ripe red fruit, full, dry or semi-dry, robust yet velvety, warm and harmonious, with minimum 24 g/L non-reducing extract.
notes: An appellation's legal organoleptic profile is not a universal cultivar average; up to 10% other permitted red grapes and multiple styles remain possible.

title: Coletta et al. — Viticultural practices, winemaking technologies and Negroamaro sensory characteristics
provenance: International Journal of Food Science & Technology 48 (2013), 2215–2227, DOI 10.1111/ijfs.12207
summary: Compares soil management, training systems and traditional, cryomaceration and ultrasound vinifications; treatments alter Negroamaro phenolic composition and sensory descriptors, with cryomaceration increasing soft-fruit and liquorice notes and ultrasound increasing violet, soft fruit and black pepper.
notes: The study does not compare Negroamaro to Vranac or prove a cultivar-wide rounded tannin level; it demonstrates why one adjective cannot define all styles.

title: English Wikipedia — Alicante Bouschet and Začinak search
provenance: Largest requested Wikipedia edition and linked cultivar material
summary: No standalone Začinak article is available. Alicante Bouschet is described as a red-fleshed teinturier whose deep colour supports blending with light red wine; the article discusses French breeding and broad international plantings but neither Serbian acreage nor a direct Začinak comparison.
notes: The infobox labels origin Spain while the history says first cultivated in France; authoritative Plantgrape is used to resolve origin. Wikipedia cannot establish Serbian area or sensory equivalence.

title: German Wikipedia — Alicante Bouschet and Začinak search
provenance: German Wikipedia cultivar article and search
summary: No standalone Začinak article was found. The Alicante Bouschet entry identifies a French 1855 Grenache × Petit Bouschet cross and says it contributes attractive red colour in blends; it supplies no Serbian planting data, Začinak must profile or direct comparison.
notes: Useful for the functional analogy and French origin only; its broad quality judgement is not used for Začinak.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia search — Začinak / Alicante Bouschet / festőszőlő
summary: No Hungarian cultivar article was found for Začinak or Alicante Bouschet, and no entry establishes their Serbian areas, pigment anatomy, wine profile or functional equivalence.
notes: Incidental mentions of Alicante Bouschet in regional pages cannot verify this two-cultivar anchor.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Vinogradarstvo u Srbiji
provenance: Serbian Wikipedia overview; no standalone articles for either comparison profile
summary: Its variety section lists both Alikant buše and Začinak among cultivars grown in Serbia. It gives no hectare date, teinturier anatomy, wine colour, astringency, blending role or direct comparison.
notes: The unquantified list is secondary corroboration; the commercial Vineyard Register is used for measured Serbian presence.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Аликант Буше and Začinak search
provenance: Russian Wikipedia cultivar article and search
summary: No Začinak article was found. Alicante Bouschet is defined as a teinturier with coloured juice and flesh, used in blends to intensify red-wine colour; the article calls it French-bred and lists major regions without documenting Serbia.
notes: The entry supports Russian terminology and the Alicante side of the analogy, not Začinak's degree of must colour or a direct match.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Alicante Bouschet and Začinak search
provenance: Croatian Wikipedia cultivar article and search
summary: No Začinak article was found. Alicante Bouschet is described as French-developed, with very dark juice and red berry interior and used mainly for blending, but the page contains an author aside and an unconfirmed permission notice and gives no Serbian acreage.
notes: Because of explicit source-quality warnings, the page is not relied on where official Plantgrape and Serbian technical sources are available.

title: CEVVIN — Začinak cultivar profile
provenance: Serbian Centre for Viticulture and Winemaking cultivar and vineyard-register profile
summary: Calls Začinak autochthonous; says its must is partly coloured and therefore places it among bojadiser cultivars. The wine is very coloured, dark red-black, extract-rich and only slightly astringent, and is mainly used to correct the colour of wines from other cultivars.
notes: The qualitative term poluobojena supports «partly coloured», not a measured weak intensity; this page's current 0.08 ha figure concerns Začinak, not Alicante Bouschet.

title: Plantgrape — Alicante Henri Bouschet
provenance: Official French national grape-variety catalogue maintained by IFV/INRAE partners
summary: Records the cultivar as obtained at Mauguio in 1855 from Grenache × Petit Bouschet and calls it a teinturier essentially used for colour input; the resulting wines have body but may be flat and lack finesse or elegance.
notes: The profile does not mention Začinak or Serbia and therefore supports only the Alicante side and the functional, not sensory, analogy.

title: Vinogradarstvo i vinarstvo Srbije — Analiza sektora proizvodnje i prerade grožđa i proizvodnje vina
provenance: 2019 CEVVIN sector study supported by the Serbian Ministry of Agriculture; Appendix 12 processes MPŠV/CEVVIN Vineyard Register data as of 1 March 2019
summary: Appendix 12 ranks cultivars in registered commercial vineyards and records Alicante Bouschet/Alicante Henri Bouschet/Alikant/Bojadiserka/Tinto Nero at 4.08 ha across 46 vineyard parcels in Serbia.
notes: This is a dated 2019 register snapshot and proves cultivation then; it does not establish unchanged 2026 area or regional distribution.

title: Avramov et al. — Vinogradar, vinogradar–rasadničar, podrumar
provenance: Digitized 1964 Serbian/Yugoslav vocational viticulture and cellar manual
summary: Describes Začinak juice as coloured and its wine as very coloured, dark and somewhat astringent, used to correct Prokupac and Skadarka colour. A separate section says Alicante Bouschet is rich in colouring matter and used to correct the colour of other red wines.
notes: The manual gives qualitative period practice rather than modern pigment measurements; its separate treatment of both cultivars supports shared role, not identity.

title: Matalj Vinarija — Začinak Bukovski 2017
provenance: Official producer technical and tasting page for a named 100% Začinak wine
summary: Documents 100% Začinak and describes the palate as soft, moderately full, fresh and fruity, with persistent but very well polished tannins balanced by lively acids.
notes: One producer vintage cannot define the cultivar, but it demonstrates both a polished-tannin style and a monovarietal exception to an exclusively blending role.

title: Pravilnik o načinu pakovanja, deklarisanja i obeležavanja mirnog vina, nekih specijalnih vina i drugih proizvoda u proizvodnji i prometu
provenance: Public republication of the Serbian rulebook issued 3 July 2023
summary: The red/rosé labelling list includes Alikant Buše with Alicante Henri Bouschet, Alikant, Alicante Bouschet and Bojadiserka synonyms, confirming contemporary legal recognition of the cultivar name in Serbia.
notes: A labelling list does not by itself prove vines are planted; the 2019 Vineyard Register table supplies the cultivation evidence.

title: Ministry of Agriculture of Serbia — Vinogradarski registar
provenance: Official Serbian Ministry of Agriculture explanation of Vineyard Register scope
summary: Explains that grape producers with parcels over 0.1 ha, and smaller producers placing grapes on the market, must enter the Vineyard Register and that CEVVIN was entrusted with register work.
notes: This establishes what the register represents but supplies no Alicante Bouschet cultivar total; use it only to interpret the 2019 sector-study table.

title: English Wikipedia — Gewürztraminer
provenance: Largest requested Wikipedia edition and linked Traminer-family material
summary: Describes Gewürztraminer as an aromatic pink-skinned cultivar, lists Traminac and Traminac Mirisavi among its names, and warns that Traminer-family names have been genetically and commercially unstable; linked Savagnin rose material distinguishes a less aromatic related form.
notes: The article has a citation-warning banner and cannot identify the cultivar behind an individual Serbian bare-Traminac label or establish a Serbian majority.

title: German Wikipedia — Gewürztraminer
summary: Treats Gewürztraminer as an aromatic form in the broader Traminer/Savagnin complex and distinguishes it from non-aromatic material despite overlapping names.
notes: It provides no Serbian label census, registry breakdown or evidence for the exact phrase «most cases».

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Tramini
summary: Uses Tramini for the Traminer/Gewürztraminer complex and supplies regional aromatic context, but does not resolve Serbian Mirisni, Crveni and Beli categories or quantify their frequency.
notes: Hungarian nomenclature cannot determine the registered cultivar behind a Serbian label.

title: Serbian Wikipedia search — Traminac / Gewürztraminer
summary: No sufficiently detailed Serbian Wikipedia cultivar article was found to distinguish Mirisni, Crveni and Beli Traminac, explain the labelling rule or establish which form predominates.
notes: Serbian identity and frequency conclusions therefore rely on ministry nomenclature, the labelling rulebook and the vineyard-register study.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Гевюрцтраминер
summary: Confirms the aromatic Gewürztraminer/Traminer relationship and uses Russian terminology for the cultivar, but contains no evidence on Serbian legal labels or the frequency of forms behind Traminac.
notes: Used only for the general anchor, not the statistical or Serbian nomenclature claims.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Traminac
summary: Shows the South Slavic regional use of Traminac and associates it with aromatic Traminer wine, but does not reliably separate every form or measure Serbian usage.
notes: The short article cannot override Serbian official nomenclature or prove a Serbian majority.

title: Plantgrape — Gewürztraminer
provenance: Official French national grape-variety catalogue maintained by IFV/INRAE partners
summary: Defines Gewürztraminer as the aromatic pink mutation of Savagnin blanc and records its rose- and lychee-led aromatic profile; the EU-name table includes Croatian Traminac for this cultivar.
notes: The EU names table does not cover non-EU Serbia and cannot establish what a bare Serbian Traminac label contains.

title: Plantgrape — Savagnin rose
provenance: Official French national grape-variety catalogue maintained by IFV/INRAE partners
summary: Maintains Savagnin rose as a separate catalogue entry, notes ampelographic similarity to Gewürztraminer and states that its wines mainly differ by lacking Gewürztraminer's spicy aromas; it has its own certified clone 763.
notes: This directly limits any blanket identity between a red/pink Traminer name and Gewürztraminer.

title: Ministry of Agriculture of Serbia — Šifarnik sorti, podloga, hibrida i područja (VV-1)
provenance: Official Serbian Ministry of Agriculture cultivar codebook supplied with the vineyard-register form
summary: One administrative line «Traminac (Grupa Traminaca)» groups Traminac, Mirisni Traminac, Crveni Traminac, Savagnin rose, Gewürztraminer, Traminer, Savagnin Blanc and Traminac beli.
notes: Administrative grouping does not assert botanical identity or disclose the frequency of its component cultivars.

title: Pravilnik o načinu pakovanja, deklarisanja i obeležavanja mirnog vina, nekih specijalnih vina i drugih proizvoda u proizvodnji i prometu
provenance: Public republication of the Serbian rulebook issued 3 July 2023
summary: The white-wine list separately gives Mirisni traminac with Gewuerztraminer/Gewurztraminer/Roter traminer, Traminac crveni with Savignin rose/Mirisavi traminac, and Traminac beli with Savagnin Blanc; a footnote permits every name or synonym in these three entries to be replaced on the label by Traminac or Traminer.
notes: The rule proves legal label ambiguity, not the market share of any of the three entries; spelling is transcribed as printed in the public text.

title: Vinogradarstvo i vinarstvo Srbije — Analiza sektora proizvodnje i prerade grožđa i proizvodnje vina
provenance: 2019 CEVVIN sector study supported by the Serbian Ministry of Agriculture; Appendix 12 processes MPŠV/CEVVIN Vineyard Register data as of 1 March 2019
summary: Appendix 12 gives only one aggregated Traminer-group row—Traminac, Mirisni, Crveni, Savagnin rose, Gewürztraminer, Traminer, Savagnin Blanc and Beli—totalling 68.98 ha and 138 vineyard parcels.
notes: The dated aggregate proves group presence but supplies neither a Gewürztraminer numerator nor a denominator for Serbian labels or wine volume.

title: wein.plus Lexicon — Gewürztraminer
provenance: Large specialist wine lexicon requested by the audit protocol
summary: Calls Gewürztraminer by far the most common Traminer variety while warning that shared synonyms across Savagnin Rose and Traminer prevent a definite cultivar conclusion from the name alone.
notes: Only openly visible text was used; international prevalence is not a measured majority of Serbian labels, hectares or wine volume.

title: Mačkov Podrum — Traminac mirisavi
provenance: Current official Serbian winery product page
summary: Provides a live Serbian commercial example using the specific name Traminac mirisavi rather than only the bare group name.
notes: One producer page confirms usage but cannot estimate how often the aromatic form occurs across Serbia.

title: Bikicki Winery — Moma Traminac Crveni
provenance: Current official Serbian winery product page
summary: Provides a live Serbian commercial counterexample explicitly presented as Traminac Crveni, demonstrating that current Traminac usage is not confined to the Mirisni/Gewürztraminer wording.
notes: The example establishes form diversity, not its prevalence; a product name alone is not genetic analysis.

title: English Wikipedia — Blaufränkisch
summary: Lists Frankovka among the alternative names of Blaufränkisch, identifies Frankovka as the Serbian name and links the cultivar to VIVC 1459; it separately describes regional style variation.
notes: The identity mapping is corroborated by VIVC and Serbia's official codebook; old planting and style figures on the page are not needed for these claims.

title: German Wikipedia — Blaufränkisch
summary: Treats Blaufränkisch, Lemberger and Limberger as names of one cultivar and includes Frankovka, Frankovka Crna and Frankovka Modra in the synonym list tied to VIVC 1459.
notes: Its style discussion is not used to claim identical wines across regions.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia — Kékfrankos
provenance: Requested Hungarian-language encyclopedia cultivar article; checked revision dated 20 July 2026
summary: The infobox and naming section explicitly place Blaufränkisch, Limberger, Frankovka and Frankovka modra among the names of Kékfrankos, treating them as one Vitis vinifera cultivar.
notes: This regional naming evidence supports identity, not a universal Hungarian or Serbian wine style.

title: Serbian Wikipedia search — Франковка / Блауфранкиш
summary: No dedicated retrievable Serbian cultivar article was found that formally maps Frankovka to Blaufränkisch; scattered wine and winery mentions do not constitute a synonym authority.
notes: The local mapping is instead directly supplied by Serbia's Ministry of Agriculture cultivar codebook.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Блауфранкиш
summary: Treats Blaufränkisch, Lemberger and Kékfrankos as regional names of one cultivar and lists the closely corresponding Slovak form Frankovka modrá; it does not specifically discuss the Serbian bare form.
notes: The Serbian name itself is verified against the national codebook and VIVC rather than inferred from the Slovak form.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Frankovka
summary: Lists Blaufränkisch, Limberger, Lemberger and Kékfrankos among the other names of Frankovka, directly supporting the regional-name correspondence.
notes: The page carries an unconfirmed content-permission notice and weak origin claims, so it is used only as required corpus evidence and not as the identity authority.

title: VIVC 1459 — BLAUFRAENKISCH
provenance: Vitis International Variety Catalogue, Julius Kühn-Institut
summary: Records BLAUFRAENKISCH as the prime name for VIVC variety 1459 and includes Frankovka, Frankovka Crna, Frankovka Modra, Kékfrankos, Lemberger and Limberger forms in its synonym set.
notes: The direct passport page returned 403 during this access, so only the publicly indexed database record and VIVC European-catalogue result were used; identity is independently confirmed by the Serbian codebook.

title: Ministry of Agriculture of Serbia — Šifarnik sorti, podloga, hibrida i područja (VV-1)
provenance: Official Serbian Ministry of Agriculture cultivar codebook supplied with the vineyard-register form
summary: The red-wine cultivar table gives code C8 as «Франковка (Limberger, Blaufränkisch)», directly joining the Serbian, German and Austrian/international names in one official entry.
notes: The codebook establishes nomenclature and register identity, not a claim that wines from different regions have identical styles.

title: wein.plus Lexicon — Frankovka
provenance: Large specialist wine lexicon requested by the audit protocol
summary: Defines Frankovka, including Frankovka Crna and Frankovka Modrá, as a synonym of the grape variety Blaufränkisch and directs the reader to that cultivar entry.
notes: Only openly visible text was used; the short synonym entry is sufficient for identity and makes no claim of uniform regional wine style.

title: Austrian Wine — Blaufränkisch
provenance: Official Austrian Wine Marketing Board cultivar profile
summary: Maintains Blaufränkisch as the official Austrian cultivar name and identifies it as a Central European variety; this supplies a primary national anchor for the international name.
notes: The page does not itself mention Frankovka; the identity bridge comes from VIVC and the Serbian codebook.

title: English Wikipedia — Bermet
summary: Describes Bermet as a Serbian aromatised dessert wine of 16–18% alcohol made in red and white forms with roughly twenty herbs and spices and a guarded Karlovci recipe; compares its aperitif use to vermouth.
notes: The page does not specifically compare Bermet with the protected Vermouth di Torino GI and relies on weak sourcing for some historical details, so it is not used for legal thresholds or sugar ranges.

title: German Wikipedia — Bermet
summary: Defines Bermet as a non-standardised Serbian and Croatian aromatised wine with producer-specific recipes and up to twenty herbs, spices and fruits including wormwood; notes production similarities to vermouth while distinguishing it from classical vermouth.
notes: It gives no controlled ranking of the nearest analogue and no specific Vermouth di Torino legal or sugar comparison.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia search — Bermet vermut
summary: No dedicated Hungarian Bermet article or retrievable passage comparing Serbian Bermet with Vermouth di Torino was found.
notes: No analogy, construction, recipe-tradition or sweetness conclusion is inferred from unrelated search results.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Бермет
summary: Presents Bermet as a traditional Karlovci sweet aromatised wine, usually 16–18% alcohol, made from red or white Fruška Gora wine with medicinal herbs and family-specific secret recipes.
notes: The article does not make a rigorous comparison to Vermouth di Torino or rank vermouth among possible explanatory anchors.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Вермут
provenance: Requested Russian-language encyclopedia comparison corpus; no dedicated Russian Bermet article was retrievable
summary: Describes vermouth as a fortified wine aromatised with wormwood, herbs and spices and notes both Turin history and sweet and dry styles, supplying only the comparison side of the book's analogy.
notes: It contains no Serbian Bermet evidence and is not used for current EU or Vermouth di Torino GI specifications.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Bermet
summary: Defines Croatian Bermet broadly as aromatised wine or spirit with wormwood and other botanicals, around 15–16% alcohol, associated with Samobor and Srijem traditions.
notes: The Croatian product tradition is not interchangeable with Serbian Bermet, and the page supplies no exact Vermouth di Torino comparison or sugar range.

title: Gorjanović et al. — Serbian aromatized wine ‘Bermet’: antioxidant activity
provenance: Journal of the Serbian Chemical Society 85(4), 517–529 (2020), DOI 10.2298/JSC190404139G
summary: Defines Serbian Bermet as red or white aromatised wine containing at least 60% wine with herb, fruit and spice extracts, 50–150 g/L sugar and usual fortification to 16–18% alcohol; documents non-standardised producer recipes and extraction methods.
notes: Its experimental recipe includes wormwood, but commercial recipes remain undisclosed, so it cannot establish wormwood in every Bermet or identify one standard formula.

title: European Commission — Aromatised wine
provenance: European Commission Directorate-General for Agriculture and Rural Development
summary: Explains that aromatised wine products add flavourings to wine products and may also include alcohol, colours and sugars; lists vermouth as an aromatised wine and names both Vermouth di Torino and Samoborski bermet among protected geographical indications.
notes: The listed bermet GI is Croatian Samoborski bermet, not Serbian Bermet; the page supports family resemblance but not legal identity or a ranking of familiar analogues.

title: Regulation (EU) No 251/2014 — consolidated text of 18 March 2026
provenance: EUR-Lex official consolidated legislation on aromatised wine products
summary: Defines the EU aromatised-wine category as based on at least 75% wine products, permits added alcohol and sweetening within the category, sets 14.5–22% alcohol for aromatised wine, and defines vermouth through characteristic flavouring from appropriate Artemisia substances.
notes: The regulation defines the legal EU category, not Serbian Bermet; the specific Torino sugar style terms come from the Italian GI specification.

title: Italian Ministry — Disciplinare di produzione Vermut di Torino / Vermouth di Torino
provenance: Ministerial Decree no. 1826 of 22 March 2017, official product specification hosted by the recognised Vermouth di Torino consortium
summary: Defines Vermouth di Torino as a Piedmont-produced aromatised wine from Italian wine products with added alcohol, primarily aromatised by Artemisia plus other herbs and spices; sets 16% to below 22% alcohol and sugar styles of extra dry below 30 g/L, dry below 50 g/L and sweet at least 130 g/L, and documents the regional tradition from the late eighteenth century.
notes: The source is a scanned PDF; all cited provisions were visually checked on rendered pages 4–6. Its protected Italian recipe cannot be projected onto Serbian Bermet.

title: Consorzio del Vermouth di Torino — L’eredità del Vermouth di Torino
provenance: Current official protection consortium recognised by the Italian Ministry of Agriculture
summary: Documents the Turin-Piedmont historical lineage, wormwood-led botanical identity and current production method: extracts of herbs, spices, flowers, seeds, roots and barks are infused in hydroalcoholic solution, then combined with sugar and wine before maturation, filtration and bottling.
notes: The consortium supports Vermouth di Torino's own local recipe tradition, showing that locality alone is not a unique contrast with Bermet.

title: English Wikipedia — Red wine
summary: Defines the international red-wine category and its violet-to-brick-red and brown colour range but contains no Serbian crno/crveno terminology, historical attestation, label-frequency trend or reader-error ranking.
notes: English red supports the familiar translation side only; it cannot justify «the whole world», because one language is not a global terminology census.

title: German Wikipedia — Rotwein
summary: Uses Rotwein for the standard category and describes red-wine production and colour, but gives no evidence about Serbian crno versus crveno, their age, trend or comprehension by Russian readers.
notes: It is one supporting example of a language using «red», not evidence that every language does so.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia search — szerb crno vino / crveno vino
summary: No retrievable Hungarian Wikipedia passage was found that explains the Serbian crno/crveno equivalence, its history, frequency trend or false-friend difficulty.
notes: A general Hungarian wine-colour term cannot establish the Serbian lexical claims.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Вино
summary: Uses both «црно вино» and «црвено вино» in headings and prose for the red-wine category and separately uses «розе»; this confirms current coexistence but not a longitudinal shift, etymology or a ranking of label traps.
notes: The page is internally inconsistent in preferred terminology, which itself supports acceptance of both forms but supplies no frequency denominator.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Красное вино
summary: Uses the Russian category красное вино and describes its colour and production, explaining why a Russian reader may expect a red adjective; it contains no study of confusion with Serbian crno or Serbian usage trends.
notes: Lexical contrast makes the false friend plausible but does not prove it is the principal or most frequent mistake.

title: Croatian Wikipedia — Crno vino
summary: Explicitly states that crno vino and crveno vino denote the same wine colour, neither is wrong, and crno vino is the traditional local-language term; also notes Spanish vino tinto as a counterexample to universal «red» naming.
notes: The article's direct sources are wine media and a retailer, so it corroborates shared usage but Serbian regulation and academic sources carry more weight for the book's Serbian claim.

title: English Wikipedia — Rosé and Dinka (grape)
provenance: Requested English-language encyclopedia pink-wine and label-ambiguity comparison; companion Dinka grape article checked
summary: The Rosé article defines the broad pink-wine category but does not discuss Serbian Ružica; the Dinka/Kövidinka article independently lists Ružica, Crvena Ružica and related forms as cultivar synonyms, exposing the label ambiguity.
notes: Companion cultivar URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinka_%28grape%29. Its old VIVC-derived synonym list is corroborated by Serbia's current rulebook.

title: German Wikipedia — Roséwein
summary: Describes rosé through limited skin contact and a range of darker and lighter methods but contains no Serbian Ružica term, historical usage, producer examples or Kövidinka homonym.
notes: The general process helps explain why darker Ružica and lighter modern rosé can differ, but does not define the Serbian naming convention.

title: Hungarian Wikipedia search — szerb Ružica rozébor Kövidinka
provenance: Requested Hungarian-language encyclopedia pink-wine and cultivar search
summary: No retrievable Hungarian Wikipedia passage was recovered that distinguishes Serbian Ružica wine from rosé or the Kövidinka cultivar.
notes: The absence is recorded explicitly; the current Serbian legal annex supplies the decisive name mapping.

title: Serbian Wikipedia — Вино
summary: Defines belo and roze wine categories and explains rosé through limited skin contact, but does not use Ružica as a wine-style term or warn that Ružica can also be a cultivar name.
notes: The primary national rulebooks and Serbian specialist sources are therefore required for Ružica.

title: Russian Wikipedia — Розовое вино
summary: Defines the Russian rosé category and short skin-contact method but has no Serbian Ružica terminology, historical claim, winery examples or cultivar ambiguity.
notes: It supports the Russian gloss розовое only, not exact equivalence between all Serbian Ružica and modern rosé styles.

title: Croatian Wikipedia search — ružica roze vino
provenance: Requested Croatian-language encyclopedia pink-wine terminology search
summary: No dedicated Croatian Wikipedia wine article was recovered that establishes Serbian Ružica as a rosé synonym or separates it from the cultivar; the obvious Rosé page is about the singer, not wine.
notes: Croatian product terminology cannot substitute for the Serbian historical and current rules in any event.

title: Federal Republic of Yugoslavia — Rulebook on wine quality and other requirements
provenance: Official Gazette of the FRY 54/1999, Articles 4–10 and 37, public copy via FAOLEX
summary: Classifies wine by quality as stono, stono with geographical origin, kvalitetno with geographical origin and vrhunsko with geographical origin; separately classifies colour as belo, ružičasto with ružica/roze in parentheses, and crno with crveno in parentheses. Article 37 defines penušavo vino through foam, pena, formed when fermentation-derived carbon dioxide is released, independently demonstrating the term's transparent wine meaning.
notes: This is a historical Yugoslav rule, not the current Serbian classification; it proves established vocabulary and semantic motivation but cannot establish current pressure thresholds, a full historical etymology, a present frequency trend or later stylistic distinctions.

title: Serbia — Rulebook on packaging, declaration and labelling of still wine and specified other wine products
provenance: Consolidated reproduction of Official Gazette RS 55/2023 and 18/2024, especially Articles 3, 9, 16, 21 and 22–23 and Annexes 5 and 8
summary: Uses the current roze/crvena heading, separately lists Ružica and its cultivar synonyms, and defines penušavo vino among distinct bubbly product types. For sulfites above 10 mg/l expressed as SO2, it requires a declaration after sadrži and permits the precise Serbian terms sulfiti or sumpor-dioksid. Article 16 normally places punilac or puni before the bottler's name and address; for GI wine it permits punjeno u … od when another producer's winery in the named area performs the bottling, identifies contract bottling through punjeno za or za … puni …, and requires a separate plant address when it differs from the bottler's registered office. Articles 22–23 make harvest year optional and allow it only when at least 85% of the product comes from grapes harvested in the stated year, with administrative evidence required for Serbian wine and narrow denominator and January/February exceptions.
notes: The rule establishes current regulated wording and directly defeats an inference from a different plant location alone. It does not prescribe the literal word berba before a vintage year, define natural wine, prove a zero-sulfite claim, measure a trend, or supply the historical etymology of penušav; the cultivar Ružica must not be confused with the pink-wine style.

title: Dejan Bulić — Vino i vinogradarstvo u Župi u srednjem veku
provenance: Institute of History Belgrade thematic proceedings Vino, tradicija i budućnost (2025)
summary: States from preserved medieval Serbian evidence that both black and white grapes were cultivated and that crno vino was more highly valued, supplying a centuries-old Serbian occurrence of the collocation.
notes: The repository returned 502 on direct opening during this check, so only the publicly indexed passage was used; the separately recorded eighteenth-century Karlovci quotation and modern linguistic research independently corroborate longevity.

title: Maurizio Barbi — Atlas boja u jedanaestom i dvanaestom izdanju rečnika Zingarelli
provenance: Peer-reviewed or scholarly lexicography proceedings paper (2024), discussion of culture-specific colour collocations
summary: Contrasts Italian, French and German wine associations with red against the Serbo-Croatian association with black in the collocation crno vino, treating it as a culture-specific colour naming pattern.
notes: The paper establishes the South Slavic semantic pattern, not uniquely Serbian origin, label frequency or the age of the phrase.

title: Hrvatski jezični portal — crven
provenance: Searchable historical and etymological dictionary portal produced by Novi Liber and SRCE
summary: Derives crven from Proto-Slavic *čьrvenъ with Old Church Slavonic, Russian and Polish cognates, establishing inherited Slavic origin rather than modern borrowing.
notes: This is a Croatian lexicographic portal, not a Serbian prescriptive dictionary; it is used only for the shared inherited etymology and is paired with Serbian current usage and regulation.

title: vino.rs — Roze vs ružica!
provenance: 2013 published answer by oenologist Ljubica Radan
summary: Says Ružica was present locally decades earlier and distinguishes it from modern rosé by longer maceration and more colour and tannin; modern rosé is lighter, while traditional Ružica had become rare on the market.
notes: This is one attributed expert explanation rather than a binding definition, but it aligns with technical differences in skin-contact duration and current traditional products.

title: Vino Kalem — Ružica
summary: Calls Ružica a traditional wine of the producer's area, describes a vivid pink-ruby colour and short skin-contact, and categorises the same product as polusuvo roze vino, directly demonstrating overlapping current usage.
notes: The page contains an internally inconsistent grape-composition field, so it is used only for the producer's naming, tradition claim and explicit rosé classification, not composition.

title: Rubin — Rubinova Ružica
provenance: Current official product page of the established Serbian producer Rubin
summary: Markets Rubinova Ružica as a dry pink wine from the domestic Prokupac cultivar and refers to a traditional production method, confirming continued use of Ružica as a product/style name.
notes: The page was blocked by a browser challenge on direct open, so only its current indexed official product text was used; it does not establish market frequency or the first historical use of the word.

title: Tourism Organisation of Novi Sad — Sremski Karlovci: vinska galaksija
provenance: Official city tourism article published in July 2021, quoting the eighteenth-century travel account of Friedrich Wilhelm von Taube
summary: Reports that eighteenth-century traveller Friedrich Wilhelm von Taube praised Karlovci wine and specifically recorded that its crno vino was of outstanding quality, supplying a dated early-modern occurrence alongside the medieval academic evidence.
notes: This is an official tourism retelling rather than the original eighteenth-century edition; it is used as corroboration, while the medieval academic source independently establishes multi-century depth.

title: Serbia Official Legal Information System — Law on Wine 41/2009 and 93/2012
provenance: Official Serbian Legal Information System, current statutory text
summary: Article 8 retains stono vino as the non-GI still-wine category and defines the regional, kvalitetno and vrhunsko geographical-origin hierarchy; Articles 5, 10 and 11 separately use grožđe for grape fruit and vinograd or vinogradarska parcela for the planted land on which grapes are produced.
notes: The official system still lists only the 2009 law and its 2012 amendment. The separately recorded May 2026 government item calls the proposed replacement a draft; legal status here is reported as checked on the access date.

title: English Wikipedia — Grape and Vineyard
summary: Separates grape as the edible fruit or berry from vineyard as a plantation of grape-bearing vines, but contains no Serbian grožđe/vinograd forms or Russian false-friend analysis.
